title: Dynamical phase selection controls compute scaling in looped transformers
summary: A looped transformer performs inference by iterating a weight-tied map, making its computation a dynamical process whose cost is set by the resulting inference dynamics. Here we show that networks with identical architecture and objective, trained to identical accuracy, nevertheless realize distinct dynamical phases depending strongly on initialization, and that the bifurcation defining each phase determines how test-time compute scales. The phases are distinguished by their bifurcation mechanisms, including a saddle-node fold and a Neimark-Sacker-type transition to bounded nonstationary motion. In the fold phase, a one-dimensional normal-form reduction predicts both the relaxation-time and spectral-gap amplitudes from local derivatives of the trained map, yielding the parameter-free relation $τ(\varepsilon)[1-λ_{\max}(-\varepsilon)]\toπ$. Composed with a regular distribution of problem difficulty, the same critical slowing down produces the workload-level tail $P(τ>N)\sim N^{-2}$. In the Neimark--Sacker phase, the fold scaling law disappears rather than merely changing its prefactor. Thus, test-time compute is not determined by architecture alone. It is governed by the dynamical phase of the solution found by training.

AI.tldr: Looped transformers performing iterative inference exhibit distinct dynamical phases depending on initialization, even with identical architecture, objective, and accuracy. The bifurcation mechanism defining each phase (saddle-node fold vs. Neimark-Sacker) determines how test-time compute scales, challenging the notion that compute is architecture-determined.
AI.motivation: To understand how the dynamical properties of looped transformer inference, rather than architecture alone, govern test-time compute scaling.
AI.method: Analysis of weight-tied iterative transformer inference as a dynamical system; classification of phases via bifurcation mechanisms (saddle-node fold and Neimark-Sacker); use of normal-form reduction to derive parameter-free relations linking relaxation time, spectral gap, and critical slowing down; statistical modeling of workload tails via composed difficulty distributions.
AI.result: Distinct dynamical phases are realized based on initialization; fold phase yields a parameter-free relation τ(ε)[1−λ_max(−ε)]→π and workload tail P(τ>N)∼N^{-2}, while the Neimark-Sacker phase eliminates the fold scaling law entirely.
AI.conclusion: Test-time compute is governed by the dynamical phase found during training rather than architecture alone, revealing initialization-dependent bifurcation structure as the key determinant.

title: Neural Renormalization Group Flow for Percolation
summary: Machine learning offers a possible route to data-driven real-space renormalization when the relevant observables are nonlocal and difficult to prescribe explicitly. We explore this idea for two-dimensional site percolation developping a supervised, scale-shared neural architecture. The model recursively applies the same learned coarse-graining rule across scales, producing a latent field from which the crossing probability is predicted, while a corresponding fine-graining decoder reconstructs the largest-cluster mask. Trained only on small lattices, the model extrapolates to substantially larger systems, recovers the spanning cluster with high fidelity, and produces observables obeying the expected finite-size scaling near the critical point. We observe that to get such performance it is key that the learned latent representation exhibits critical fluctuations and scale-dependent flows consistent with the renormalization-group structure of percolation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a supervised, scale-shared neural architecture for data-driven real-space renormalization of two-dimensional site percolation, trained on small lattices yet extrapolating to larger systems, recovering spanning clusters, and producing observables with correct finite-size scaling near criticality.
AI.motivation: Machine learning provides a route to data-driven real-space renormalization when relevant observables are nonlocal and hard to prescribe explicitly, as is the case for site percolation.
AI.method: A supervised, scale-shared neural architecture recursively applies the same learned coarse-graining rule across scales to produce a latent field for predicting crossing probability, paired with a fine-graining decoder that reconstructs the largest-cluster mask.
AI.result: Trained on small lattices, the model extrapolates to larger systems, recovers the spanning cluster with high fidelity, and produces observables exhibiting expected finite-size scaling near the critical point. Performance depends critically on the latent representation exhibiting critical fluctuations and scale-dependent flows consistent with the renormalization-group structure of percolation.
AI.conclusion: A well-designed scale-shared neural architecture can learn an effective renormalization-group-like representation for percolation that generalizes across scales, with the learned latent space carrying the physical signatures of criticality.

title: Low-temperature magnetism and spin dynamics in the disordered triangular-lattice Yb$^{3+}$ compound LiCaYb$_5$(BO$_3$)$_6$
summary: The interplay between geometric frustration, spin--orbit coupling, and structural disorder can give rise to unconventional magnetic ground states in rare-earth triangular-lattice magnets. We report low-temperature magnetic and $^7$Li NMR investigations of the disordered triangular-lattice compound LiCaYb$_5$(BO$_3$)$_6$ (LCYBO). Rietveld refinement confirms a hexagonal $P6_522$ structure with partial Ca/Yb antisite disorder and fractional Li occupancy. Magnetic susceptibility and magnetization measurements indicate a well-isolated effective $J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2$ Kramers doublet with weak antiferromagnetic interactions ($θ_{\mathrm{CW}} \approx -0.54$~K). The specific heat reveals a weak anomaly near 0.43 K, suggesting the development of short-range correlated magnetism rather than conventional long-range order. $^7$Li NMR spectra broaden strongly upon cooling, consistent with increasingly inhomogeneous internal magnetic fields. The spin-lattice relaxation exhibits two relaxation components consistent with disorder-induced distributions of local magnetic environments arising from antisite disorder and competing exchange pathways. Our results establish LCYBO as a structurally disordered frustrated triangular-lattice magnet with correlated low-energy spin dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the disordered triangular-lattice compound LiCaYb5(BO3)6 (LCYBO) using low-temperature magnetic measurements and 7Li NMR, revealing a J_eff=1/2 Kramers doublet system with weak antiferromagnetic interactions, short-range correlated magnetism, and disorder-induced inhomogeneous spin dynamics without long-range order.
AI.motivation: To understand how geometric frustration, spin-orbit coupling, and structural disorder collectively give rise to unconventional magnetic ground states in rare-earth triangular-lattice magnets, using LCYBO as a model system.
AI.method: The study combines Rietveld refinement of X-ray/neutron diffraction to establish the crystal structure (hexagonal P6_522 with Ca/Yb antisite disorder and fractional Li occupancy), low-temperature magnetic susceptibility and magnetization measurements, specific heat measurements, and 7Li NMR spectroscopy including spin-lattice relaxation measurements.
AI.result: LCYBO exhibits a well-isolated J_eff=1/2 Kramers doublet with weak antiferromagnetic interactions (theta_CW ≈ -0.54 K). A weak specific heat anomaly near 0.43 K indicates short-range correlated magnetism rather than long-range order. 7Li NMR spectra broaden strongly on cooling, and spin-lattice relaxation shows two components reflecting disorder-induced distributions of local magnetic environments.
AI.conclusion: LCYBO is established as a structurally disordered frustrated triangular-lattice magnet with correlated low-energy spin dynamics, where antisite disorder and competing exchange pathways create inhomogeneous local magnetic environments that suppress long-range order and promote short-range correlations.

title: Krylov Break Times from an Inhomogeneous Lieb--Robinson Light Cone
summary: Krylov and Lanczos approximations are used in quantum dynamics, quantum subspace methods, and Hamiltonian learning. A practical question is how long an $m$-dimensional Krylov truncation can be trusted. We argue that this time is fixed by causal propagation on the associated Jacobi chain. The relevant distance is not the Krylov index itself, but the inhomogeneous transport metric $ρ(m,n) = \sum_{j=\min(m,n)}^{\max(m,n)-1} 1/b_j$, where $b_j$ is the Lanczos hopping across the bond $j \leftrightarrow j+1$. We prove a Lieb--Robinson bound in this metric. Its small-weight limit gives the velocity $v_{\rm LR} = 2$, meaning that propagation is exponentially suppressed outside the cone $ρ(m,n) \simeq 2|t|$. The error of a finite Krylov approximation to the return amplitude is a round-trip effect: information has to travel from the probe to the truncation boundary and back. Combining the Lieb--Robinson bound with Duhamel's formula yields a lower bound on the error of the truncated dynamics. For a fixed tolerance $ε$, let the break time $t_\ast(m;ε)$ denote the longest time for which the $m$-dimensional truncation is guaranteed to reproduce the exact return amplitude within error $ε$. We show that $t_\ast(m;ε) \ge τ_m[1-o(1)]$, where $τ_m = ρ(0,m) = \sum_{j<m} 1/b_j$. When the probe spreads along the chain, this lower bound is also tight, so $t_\ast(m) \simeq τ_m$. The situation is different when the probe excites only a localized part of the spectrum, or a part already resolved by the truncation. In this case, essentially no signal reaches the boundary. Beyond a state-dependent Krylov dimension $m_\ast$, the approximation can therefore remain accurate at all times, and the break time is effectively infinite. Numerical tests on spin chains and random Jacobi matrices support $t_\ast(m) \simeq τ_m$ in the transport-limited regime.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes rigorous bounds on the validity time of finite Krylov truncations in quantum dynamics. The break time is set by causal propagation on the Jacobi chain, governed by the inhomogeneous transport metric ρ(m,n) = Σ_{j=min(m,n)}^{max(m,n)-1} 1/b_j. A Lieb–Robinson bound in this metric yields the break time lower bound t_*(m;ε) ≥ τ_m[1-o(1)] with τ_m = ρ(0,m). When the probe spreads along the chain, this bound is tight (t_* ≃ τ_m); when the excitation is localized in spectrum, the break time is effectively infinite beyond a state-dependent Krylov dimension.
AI.motivation: Krylov and Lanczos methods are widely used in quantum dynamics, quantum subspace methods, and Hamiltonian learning, but the practical question of how long an m-dimensional Krylov truncation remains trustworthy was unresolved. Establishing rigorous error/validity bounds is essential for reliable application of these methods.
AI.method: The paper combines causal propagation analysis on the Jacobi chain with a newly defined inhomogeneous transport metric ρ(m,n). It proves a Lieb–Robinson bound in this metric (with small-weight limit velocity v_LR = 2), and combines it with Duhamel's formula to derive a lower bound on the error of truncated dynamics.
AI.result: The break time for a finite m-dimensional Krylov truncation satisfies t_*(m;ε) ≥ τ_m[1-o(1)], where τ_m = ρ(0,m). This bound is tight when the probe spreads along the chain (t_* ≃ τ_m). However, when the probe excites only a localized spectral part already resolved by the truncation, essentially no signal reaches the boundary, making the break time effectively infinite beyond a state-dependent Krylov dimension m_*. Numerical tests on spin chains and random Jacobi matrices support t_* ≃ τ_m in the transport-limited regime.
AI.conclusion: The validity time of Krylov truncations is fundamentally determined by causal (light-cone) propagation on the Jacobi chain, with the relevant distance being the inhomogeneous transport metric rather than the Krylov index. The break time scales as τ_m in the transport-limited regime, but can be infinite for spectrally localized excitations, providing a complete characterization of when finite Krylov approximations can be trusted.

title: Least Variable Quantum Counting Processes
summary: Counting processes provide a fundamental description of stochastic events ranging from photon detection to clock ticks. A central question is how accurately such events can be timed when only finite memory resources are available. Here, we investigate this problem within a general framework of finite-dimensional classical and quantum counting processes. We derive a rigorous finite-memory variance bound obeyed by every classical $d$-state counting process, which is tight and saturated by a discrete Erlang-type ladder process. Through numerical optimization, we identify quantum counting processes that violate this classical bound, achieving smaller first-tick fluctuations than any classical process with the same memory size and mean tick time. For the qubit case, we further derive an analytical large-mean bound within a single-Kraus no-tick family, showing that the quantum advantage persists asymptotically within this class. The optimized quantum processes exhibit coherent conditioned dynamics and approach a continuous-time quantum-jump description as the mean increases. Our results establish a finite-memory quantum advantage in temporal precision and connect discrete-time counting processes with continuous-time quantum timekeeping.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how accurately stochastic events can be timed using finite-memory classical and quantum counting processes, deriving a tight classical variance bound, identifying quantum processes that violate it, and establishing a finite-memory quantum advantage in temporal precision.
AI.motivation: To determine how accurately stochastic events can be timed given finite memory resources, and whether quantum systems can outperform classical ones in such temporal precision tasks.
AI.method: The authors derive a rigorous finite-memory variance bound for classical d-state counting processes that is tight and saturated by a discrete Erlang-type ladder process. They use numerical optimization to search for quantum counting processes that violate this bound, and derive an analytical large-mean bound for the qubit case within a single-Kraus no-tick family.
AI.result: Quantum counting processes are identified that achieve smaller first-tick fluctuations than any classical process with the same memory size and mean tick time, violating the classical bound. The quantum advantage persists asymptotically in the qubit case, and optimized quantum processes exhibit coherent conditioned dynamics approaching continuous-time quantum-jump behavior as the mean increases.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a finite-memory quantum advantage in temporal precision and connect discrete-time counting processes with continuous-time quantum timekeeping.

title: Dynamics of local quantum information in random unitary circuits
summary: The physics of information scrambling in quantum many-body systems is intimately related to thermalisation and emergence of chaos. However, its standard characterisation through bipartite entanglement or operator growth remains inherently coarse-grained, obscuring the spatiotemporal anatomy of how quantum information flows between different regions of the system and across various length scales. In this work, we develop a theory for the dynamics of local information in local random unitary circuits which resolves the fine-grained microscopic structures of local information flow in such systems. Using the framework of information lattice which systematises the information content at each length scale within each subsystem, we identify a distribution of length scales at which information resides and obtain the dynamics of the distribution. For Haar-random circuits with infinite local Hilbert-space dimensions, we map this dynamics onto an exact classical stochastic process which reveals that this distribution is described by a Tracy-Widom form which moves ballistically in time ($ \propto t$) toward larger scales, accompanied by a $\sim t^{1/3}$ broadening. We also find the same qualitative behaviour for random Clifford circuits acting on qubits. The similar scaling behaviour in two rather different settings hints strongly towards the universality of our results. In the case of Clifford circuits, we develop a phenomenological Markov process for the dynamics of the stabiliser generators in a specific gauge which confirms the Tracy-Widom distribution and the $t^{1/3}$ scaling of the fluctuations. Ultimately, our results establish the universal properties of the dynamics of local quantum information in a length scale-resolved fashion and provide a possible route towards bridging exact microscopic theories for information dynamics with emergent hydrodynamic descriptions of information flow.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a theory for the fine-grained dynamics of local quantum information in local random unitary circuits using an "information lattice" framework that resolves information content at each length scale. The authors find that the distribution of information length scales moves ballistically in time toward larger scales with Tracy-Widom statistics and t^(1/3) broadening, observed in both Haar-random circuits with infinite local Hilbert space and random Clifford circuits, suggesting universality.
AI.motivation: Standard characterizations of information scrambling through bipartite entanglement or operator growth are coarse-grained and obscure the spatiotemporal anatomy of how quantum information flows between different regions and across length scales. The authors aim to resolve the fine-grained microscopic structure of local information flow in quantum many-body systems.
AI.method: The authors employ the framework of an "information lattice" to systematize information content at each length scale within each subsystem. For Haar-random circuits with infinite local Hilbert-space dimensions, they map the dynamics onto an exact classical stochastic process. For random Clifford circuits on qubits, they develop a phenomenological Markov process for the dynamics of stabiliser generators in a specific gauge.
AI.result: The distribution of information length scales is described by a Tracy-Widom form that moves ballistically in time (~t) toward larger scales, accompanied by ~t^(1/3) broadening. This qualitative behavior is observed in both Haar-random circuits (via exact stochastic process mapping) and random Clifford circuits (via stabiliser gauge Markov process), suggesting universality across these two different settings.
AI.conclusion: The results establish universal properties of the dynamics of local quantum information in a length scale-resolved fashion, and provide a route toward bridging exact microscopic theories for information dynamics with emergent hydrodynamic descriptions of information flow.

title: Fast GHZ encoding with $1-o(1)$ fidelity
summary: We prove that $(1-o(1))$-fidelity $N$-qubit Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger (GHZ) encoding can be performed in time $O(\log N/N)$ using all-to-all 2-local Hamiltonians with bounded 2-qubit interaction terms. This saturates the theoretical lower bound $Ω(\log N/N)$, and by rescaling, also saturates the lower bound on signaling time for Hamiltonians with power-law interaction strengths $1/r^γ$, $γ<d$ in dimension $d$. The protocol uses spin-squeezing dynamics combined with quantum signal processing.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that GHZ state encoding with (1-o(1)) fidelity can be performed in O(log N/N) time using all-to-all 2-local Hamiltonians with bounded interaction terms, saturating the theoretical lower bound Ω(log N/N). The protocol combines spin-squeezing dynamics with quantum signal processing and also saturates signaling time bounds for power-law interacting Hamiltonians.
AI.motivation: The goal is to determine the fundamental speed limit for preparing GHZ states (a key resource for quantum information processing) using physically realizable 2-local Hamiltonians, and to determine if the theoretical lower bound on encoding time can be achieved.
AI.method: The authors develop a protocol that combines spin-squeezing dynamics with quantum signal processing techniques to achieve near-optimal GHZ encoding under all-to-all 2-local Hamiltonians with bounded 2-qubit interactions.
AI.result: The protocol achieves (1-o(1))-fidelity GHZ encoding in O(log N/N) time, saturating the Ω(log N/N) lower bound. Via rescaling, it also saturates the lower bound on signaling time for power-law interacting Hamiltonians with interaction strength 1/r^γ for γ<d in dimension d.
AI.conclusion: The established time-optimality proves that GHZ encoding can be performed at the fundamental speed limit dictated by the Lieb-Robinson-type bounds for both all-to-all and power-law interacting systems, demonstrating that no fundamental gap exists between achievable and theoretical limits.

title: Lieb-Schultz-Mattis Constraints for Quantum Channels: A Spacetime-Duality View
summary: Quantum anomalies strongly constrain the possible behavior of many-body systems. A prime example is the Lieb-Schultz-Mattis (LSM) theorem, which relates UV symmetry and filling constraints to IR features of the energy spectrum and ground-state structure. Here, we ask how LSM constraints shape dynamical signatures and temporal correlations in open quantum systems. Using a spacetime duality, we show that the Liouvillian of a $d$-dimensional repeated quantum channel with a mixed anomaly between strong $S$ and weak $G$ symmetry can be mapped to a $(d{+}1)$-dimensional mixed-state symmetry-protected topological (mSPT) phase. Under this correspondence, the initial and steady states of the channel are identified with boundary states of the higher-dimensional mSPT in the presence of bulk projection. We further introduce the twisted Renyi-$N$ correlator (TRNC) as a probe of temporal correlations in the channel and demonstrate that it is dual to the mSPT strange correlator, providing a direct bulk-boundary route to diagnose long-range temporal order implied by the LSM anomaly. Finally, we identify the \textit{Liouvillian singular spectrum}, rather than the Liouvillian spectrum itself, as a more fundamental diagnostic of quantum anomalies, and show that it is dual to the operator entanglement spectrum of the mSPT.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the Lieb-Schultz-Mattis (LSM) theorem to open quantum systems, using spacetime duality to map the Liouvillian of a d-dimensional repeated quantum channel with mixed anomalies to a (d+1)-dimensional mixed-state symmetry-protected topological (mSPT) phase. The authors introduce the twisted Renyi-N correlator (TRNC) and the Liouvillian singular spectrum as new diagnostics of quantum anomalies and long-range temporal order.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to understand how LSM-type quantum anomaly constraints manifest in the dynamics and temporal correlations of open quantum systems, rather than just in static energy spectra and ground states as traditionally studied.
AI.method: The authors employ a spacetime duality to map the Liouvillian of a repeated quantum channel (with mixed S-strong and G-weak symmetry anomaly) to a higher-dimensional mSPT phase. They introduce the twisted Renyi-N correlator (TRNC) as a probe of temporal correlations, dual to the mSPT strange correlator, and identify the Liouvillian singular spectrum as a diagnostic dual to the operator entanglement spectrum of the mSPT.
AI.result: The Liouvillian of the channel maps to a (d+1)-dimensional mSPT phase, with initial and steady states identified as boundary states under bulk projection. The TRNC is shown to be dual to the mSPT strange correlator, enabling diagnosis of long-range temporal order from the LSM anomaly. The Liouvillian singular spectrum is shown to be a more fundamental diagnostic than the Liouvillian spectrum itself, dual to the operator entanglement spectrum.
AI.conclusion: LSM-type quantum anomalies manifest in open quantum systems through distinctive dynamical signatures and temporal correlations, which can be systematically diagnosed via spacetime-duality-inspired quantities such as the TRNC and the Liouvillian singular spectrum.

title: Bosonic Encodings for Hermite-Galerkin Discretizations of High-Dimensional PDEs and Bayesian Inverse Problems
summary: The Koopman-von Neumann framework has been proposed to design quantum algorithms for non-linear dynamics. It maps a non-linear ordinary differential equation to a linear partial differential equation (PDE) governing a probability amplitude. Previous works represents this amplitude in the Hermite-function basis, equivalently as a bosonic state, and truncates the total Hermite degree to obtain a representation over $Θ(m\log N)$ qubits, where $N$ is the number of variables and $m$ the truncation order. We extend this approach to a broader class of linear PDEs whose differential operators have a structured polynomial form. We prove convergence of the truncation for both time-dependent dynamics and gapped ground-state problems under explicit regularity and stability assumptions. We then introduce a qubit encoding that supports efficient block encodings of the truncated operators. Finally, we apply the framework to Bayesian inverse problems with Gaussian priors and observation noise, reducing posterior-state preparation to the preparation of a structured Hamiltonian's ground state.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the Koopman-von Neumann framework for quantum algorithms of non-linear dynamics to a broader class of linear PDEs with structured polynomial differential operators, proves truncation convergence for both time-dependent and ground-state problems, introduces a qubit encoding enabling efficient block encodings, and applies the framework to Bayesian inverse problems.
AI.motivation: Previous Koopman-von Neumann approaches map non-linear ODEs to linear PDEs represented in a Hermite-function basis, but are limited to the specific structure of that setting, truncating to O(m log N) qubits. The authors aim to generalize this approach to a wider class of linear PDEs with polynomial-structured differential operators and to provide rigorous convergence guarantees for truncation—which were previously lacking—while also extending practical applicability to Bayesian inverse problems.
AI.method: The framework represents the PDE solution amplitude in a Hermite/bosonic basis and truncates the total Hermite degree. The authors (1) extend this to general linear PDEs with structured polynomial differential operators, (2) prove truncation convergence under explicit regularity and stability assumptions for both time-dependent dynamics and gapped ground-state problems, (3) design a qubit encoding supporting efficient block encodings of the truncated operators, and (4) apply the framework to Bayesian inverse problems with Gaussian priors and observation noise by reducing posterior-state preparation to ground-state preparation of a structured Hamiltonian.
AI.result: The paper provides convergence proofs for the truncation procedure under stated assumptions, demonstrates efficient qubit encodings and block encodings for the truncated operators, and establishes a connection between Bayesian posterior-state preparation and structured Hamiltonian ground-state preparation within the Koopman-von Neumann framework.
AI.conclusion: The generalized Koopman-von Neumann framework broadens the scope of quantum algorithms for linear PDEs with polynomial structure, offers theoretical guarantees for truncation in both dynamical and ground-state settings, and opens a path to quantum algorithms for Bayesian inverse problems through structured Hamiltonian ground-state preparation.

title: Fault-tolerant quantum computation cannot be achieved with constant spacetime overhead
summary: The threshold theorem states that quantum computations can be made reliable below a physical error threshold, at the cost of additional physical qubits and circuit depth. Recent work has reduced these space and time overheads to polylogarithmic or nearly logarithmic scalings, but whether the cumulative spacetime overhead can be constant has remained unclear. Here, we show that even for the simplest task of preserving quantum information in a quantum memory, under an optimistic noise model and allowing general adaptive protocols, there is an unavoidable logarithmic contribution to the cumulative spacetime overhead. This additional cost can nevertheless be shared among many logical qubits, so sufficiently wide computations, including standard implementations of Shor's algorithm, may still achieve constant relative overhead. We further give a positive-rate CSS code construction that attains the memory bound, identify sufficient conditions under which the same scaling extends from quantum memory to fault-tolerant circuit implementations, and derive circuit-size bounds for subsystem spacetime codes. Our work establishes fundamental limits on the resources required for quantum fault tolerance.

AI.tldr: This paper proves a fundamental lower bound: even for the simplest task of preserving quantum information in a quantum memory, there is an unavoidable logarithmic contribution to the cumulative spacetime overhead under optimistic noise and general adaptive protocols. However, this cost can be amortized across many logical qubits, so wide computations like Shor's algorithm may still achieve constant relative overhead. The authors also provide a positive-rate CSS code achieving the memory bound and derive circuit-size bounds for subsystem spacetime codes.
AI.motivation: The threshold theorem ensures reliable quantum computation below a physical error threshold, but the question of whether cumulative spacetime overhead can be made constant has remained open. The authors aim to establish fundamental resource limits on quantum fault tolerance, specifically addressing whether the logarithmic scaling can be avoided entirely.
AI.method: The authors analyze the cumulative spacetime overhead of quantum fault tolerance under an optimistic noise model, allowing general adaptive protocols. They prove an unavoidable logarithmic overhead for quantum memory, construct a positive-rate CSS code that attains this memory bound, and identify sufficient conditions under which the same scaling extends from quantum memory to fault-tolerant circuit implementations. They also derive circuit-size bounds for subsystem spacetime codes.
AI.result: Even for the simplest task of quantum memory preservation, a logarithmic contribution to cumulative spacetime overhead is unavoidable. This overhead can be shared among many logical qubits, so sufficiently wide computations—including standard implementations of Shor's algorithm—may still achieve constant relative overhead. A positive-rate CSS code construction attains the memory bound, and circuit-size bounds for subsystem spacetime codes are derived.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes fundamental limits on the resources required for quantum fault tolerance, showing that while logarithmic spacetime overhead is not universally avoidable, it can be amortized in sufficiently wide computations, providing a nuanced resource landscape for quantum error correction.

title: Quantizing the guiding center: do quantization and coarse graining commute?
summary: We develop a nonperturbative, group-theoretic quantization of the effective guiding center theory of a charged particle drifting in a magnetic field in two spatial dimensions, and compare the resulting quantum theory with a corresponding coarse graining of the underlying microscopic theory. In the classical effective theory, the small gyro motion is not resolved, while the motion of the center of the gyro orbit remains observable. The reduced phase space is the physical space itself, so quantization leads to noncommuting spatial coordinates, and the effective theory loses access to the metric structure of physical space, retaining only its area structure. By formulating a prescription to match between the microscopic and effective quantum theories, we find that the predictions of the quantized effective theory are generally consistent with those of the microscopic theory. However, for closed isomagnetic contours the effective theory predicts a quantization of ``radius'', a spatial discreteness absent from the microscopic theory. This illustrates that quantization of an effective theory may yield spurious nonperturbative predictions, even if that quantum theory shows no internal signs of breakdown.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a nonperturbative, group-theoretic quantization of the effective guiding-center theory for a charged particle in a 2D magnetic field, compares it with coarse-grained microscopic theory, and finds that while predictions generally agree, the effective theory spuriously predicts quantized "radius" for closed isomagnetic contours—a discreteness absent in the microscopic theory—illustrating that quantized effective theories can yield spurious nonperturbative predictions without internal signs of breakdown.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether quantizing an effective (coarse-grained) classical theory yields reliable nonperturbative predictions by systematically comparing the quantized guiding-center effective theory with the corresponding coarse-grained microscopic quantum theory.
AI.method: A group-theoretic, nonperturbative quantization of the effective guiding-center theory is formulated; the reduced phase space is physical space itself, leading to noncommuting spatial coordinates and loss of metric structure (only area structure retained). A matching prescription between microscopic and effective quantum theories is then constructed and used to compare their predictions.
AI.result: The quantized effective theory's predictions are generally consistent with the microscopic theory. However, for closed isomagnetic contours, the effective theory predicts a spatial discreteness—quantization of "radius"—that is not present in the microscopic theory.
AI.conclusion: Quantization of an effective theory can produce spurious nonperturbative predictions (e.g., spurious spatial quantization), even when the effective quantum theory shows no internal inconsistency, highlighting the need for matching to the microscopic theory to validate such predictions.

title: Exploiting overcompleteness of Platonic-solid POVMs for shadow estimation
summary: Accurately estimating expectation values of observables from a finite number of measurement shots is a central challenge in quantum information science. Informationally overcomplete measurements provide a route to reduce estimation variance through optimized classical post-processing. However, the interplay between measurement geometry and dual-frame construction remains largely unexplored. In this work, we study Platonic solid POVMs ---highly symmetric, overcomplete single-qubit measurements whose effects correspond to the vertices of the five Platonic solids on the Bloch sphere--- for the estimation of molecular Hamiltonians. Using $k$-locally optimal dual frames, we show that the geometry of the POVM can have a non-trivial and non-monotonic effect on the estimation variance. We further propose a joint optimization of the POVM orientation and effect weights using a classical proxy state, either a product state or a Matrix Product State (MPS) approximation. We demonstrate that optimized Platonic solid POVMs can outperform standard randomized Pauli measurements, provided the MPS bond dimension is sufficient to faithfully represent the target state. These results reveal a trade-off between classical preprocessing and estimation accuracy, suggesting a practical route to improved observable estimation on near-term quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: The paper studies Platonic solid POVMs (highly symmetric, overcomplete single-qubit measurements) for estimating molecular Hamiltonian expectation values, showing that measurement geometry has a non-trivial, non-monotonic effect on estimation variance when combined with k-locally optimal dual frames. Joint optimization of POVM orientation and effect weights using classical proxy states (product or MPS) allows these measurements to outperform standard randomized Pauli measurements, given sufficient MPS bond dimension.
AI.motivation: Accurate estimation of observable expectation values from finite measurement shots is a central challenge in quantum information science. While informationally overcomplete measurements can reduce estimation variance through optimized classical post-processing, the interplay between measurement geometry and dual-frame construction has been largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors study Platonic solid POVMs (where effects correspond to vertices of the five Platonic solids on the Bloch sphere) for molecular Hamiltonian estimation. They use k-locally optimal dual frames and propose joint optimization of the POVM orientation and effect weights using a classical proxy state—either a product state or a Matrix Product State (MPS) approximation.
AI.result: The geometry of the POVM produces a non-trivial and non-monotonic effect on estimation variance. Optimized Platonic solid POVMs outperform standard randomized Pauli measurements when the MPS bond dimension is sufficient to faithfully represent the target state.
AI.conclusion: The results reveal a trade-off between classical preprocessing and estimation accuracy, suggesting a practical route to improved observable estimation on near-term quantum hardware.

title: Enhancing the phase sensitivity of a Mach-Zehnder interferometer beyond the Heisenberg limit through dynamic squeezing
summary: We propose a method to enhance the phase sensitivity of a Mach-Zehnder interferometer, independent of its input states. This is achieved by applying squeezing sequences to one arm of the interferometer. By alternating between squeezing along orthogonal quadratures, we demonstrate that the phase sensitivity of a Mach-Zehnder interferometer can be generically enhanced. Since this enhancement is independent of the input states, the proposed dynamic squeezing method allows for further improvement in phase sensitivity when combined with non-classical input states. We compare the dynamic squeezing approach with existing quantum sensing protocols and show that super-Heisenberg scaling can be achieved. Finally, we demonstrate that the scheme is robust against moderate photon loss.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dynamic squeezing method for enhancing the phase sensitivity of a Mach-Zehnder interferometer by alternating squeezing along orthogonal quadratures in one arm. This enhancement is input-state independent, can be combined with non-classical states, achieves super-Heisenberg scaling, and remains robust against moderate photon loss.
AI.motivation: To improve the phase sensitivity of Mach-Zehnder interferometers in a way that does not depend on the specific input states used, enabling broader applicability and further gains when combined with existing non-classical state preparation techniques.

title: Misunderstanding Convivial Solipsism: the Necessity of a Perspectival Logic
summary: Convivial Solipsism is easily misunderstood. Because it denies the absoluteness of observed events while preserving the universality of quantum mechanics, it invites objections that are often formulated in a classical, non-perspectival language. Such objections appear powerful only because they smuggle back into the discussion the very assumptions that Convivial Solipsism rejects. This article reconstructs a family of misunderstandings that arise in discussions of Convivial Solipsism, especially in connection with Wigner's friend and extended Wigner's friend scenarios. The aim is not merely defensive. The objections are useful because they identify the conceptual discipline required by any interpretation that takes non-absolute facts seriously. The central claim is that observational facts must be indexed to perspectives. A statement such as "the friend saw outcome A" is not a complete factual statement within Convivial Solipsism. It must be reformulated as "from the friend's perspective, the friend saw outcome A" or "from Wigner's perspective, the friend reported outcome B." The mistake consists in removing these indices and then treating the resulting expressions as if they belonged to a single global factual domain. This leads to apparent contradictions and to false dilemmas concerning consciousness, communication, other minds, and intersubjectivity. When that is taken into account, it appears that Convivial Solipsism is not a retreat into psychological solipsism, but a discipline of perspectival discourse. It is also shown that perspectival logic stands to classical logic as the quantum calculus of probability stands to Kolmogorovian probability theory.

AI.tldr: This paper defends Convivial Solipsism against common misunderstandings by showing that objections arise from smuggling in classical, non-perspectival assumptions. The central claim is that observational facts must be indexed to perspectives, and that perspectival logic relates to classical logic as quantum probability calculus relates to Kolmogorovian probability.
AI.motivation: Convivial Solipsism is often misunderstood and rejected based on objections formulated in classical, non-perspectival language. These objections appear powerful only because they implicitly restore the very assumptions the interpretation rejects. The paper aims to clarify these misunderstandings and show they actually reveal the conceptual discipline required for any interpretation that takes non-absolute facts seriously.
AI.method: The paper reconstructs a family of misunderstandings in Convivial Solipsism, particularly in Wigner's friend and extended Wigner's friend scenarios. It demonstrates that statements like "the friend saw outcome A" must be reformulated with explicit perspective indices (e.g., "from the friend's perspective..."). It then draws an analogy between perspectival logic and classical logic on one hand, and quantum probability calculus and Kolmogorovian probability on the other.
AI.result: The apparent contradictions and false dilemmas in Convivial Solipsism (concerning consciousness, communication, other minds, intersubjectivity) dissolve once perspective indices are properly maintained. Convivial Solipsism is shown to be not a retreat into psychological solipsism but a discipline of perspectival discourse, with perspectival logic structurally analogous to quantum probability theory.
AI.conclusion: Convivial Solipsism is a coherent interpretive framework when correctly understood: observational facts are perspective-indexed, and the apparent paradoxes raised against it stem from illicitly removing these indices. The interpretation is not solipsistic in the psychological sense but offers a disciplined perspectival account of quantum mechanics.

title: Recovery-Free CHSH Nonlocality with Particle Loss
summary: Can CHSH nonlocality survive particle loss without applying an explicit recovery operation? In principle, any deterministic recovery can be absorbed into the measurement. Operationally, we show that the answer depends on the allowed measurements on the lossy system. We distinguish flagged erasure, in which each lost particle leaves a detectable record, from unflagged deletion, in which no such record remains. For flagged erasure and survival probability $η>1/2$, using known quantum-capacity results, we show measurements that asymptotically approach the quantum maximum $2\sqrt2$. In contrast, for $η\le1/2$, CHSH violation is impossible for both loss models. Then, we construct explicit recovery-free protocols using permutation-invariant encodings built from $n$-qubit Dicke states $| D_N^n\rangle$ and measurements on the surviving particles. A one-excitation $(N=1)$ encoding violates CHSH for $η>1/\sqrt{2}$. Increasing the excitation number $N$ yields a family of protocols that violates CHSH for $η>η_G=(\sqrt{5}-1)/2$, with the asymptotic golden ratio approached as $N \to \infty$. Finally, we present a sparse-deletion binomial PI protocol that guarantees CHSH violation for up to $O(\sqrt n)$ deletion errors. Our results distinguish fundamental limits imposed by loss from those set by explicit measurements without recovery.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether CHSH nonlocality can survive particle loss in quantum systems without explicit recovery operations. The authors distinguish between flagged erasure (detectable loss) and unflagged deletion (undetectable loss), showing that for flagged erasure with survival probability η>1/2, measurements can asymptotically approach the quantum maximum of 2√2, while for η≤1/2, CHSH violation is impossible in both loss models. They construct explicit recovery-free protocols using permutation-invariant encodings based on n-qubit Dicke states, achieving CHSH violation thresholds down to the golden ratio η_G=(√5−1)/2 for large excitation numbers, and a sparse-deletion binomial protocol guaranteeing violation for up to O(√n) deletion errors.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to determine whether quantum nonlocality (specifically CHSH inequality violation) can survive particle loss in practical quantum systems without requiring an explicit recovery operation, distinguishing fundamental physical limits from operational constraints set by measurement choices on lossy systems.
AI.method: The authors distinguish two loss models: flagged erasure (each lost particle leaves a detectable record) and unflagged deletion (no record remains). They use known quantum-capacity results to show that for flagged erasure with η>1/2, measurements can asymptotically approach the QM maximum of 2√2, while η≤1/2 prohibits CHSH violation in both models. They then construct explicit recovery-free protocols using permutation-invariant encodings built from n-qubit Dicke states |D_N^n⟩ with measurements on surviving particles, including a one-excitation encoding for η>1/√2 and a family with increasing excitation number N approaching the golden ratio threshold for large N. They also present a sparse-deletion binomial protocol for bounded deletion errors.

Explicit protocols are constructed: a one-excitation Dicke encoding violates CHSH for η>1/√2, while increasing excitation number N yields violation for η>η_G=(√5−1)/2, approaching the golden ratio in the asymptotic limit. A sparse-deletion binomial PI protocol guarantees CHSH violation for up to O(√n) deletion errors.

It establishes that nonlocality can survive considerable loss, with thresholds depending sensitively on whether loss is flagged or unflagged and on the encoding strategy used, providing both upper and lower bounds on achievable CHSH violation under loss.

title: The Role of Geometric Analysis in Interferometer Design and Optimization for Gravitational Quantum Entanglement
summary: The pursuit of a quantum theory of gravity, aiming to unify general relativity and quantum mechanics, remains one of the most enduring challenges in physics. Because of the extreme energy scales associated with the Planck regime, direct experimental evidence for quantum gravity remains elusive. However, recent proposals suggest that quantum entanglement between two massive particles may provide a pathway to probe the quantum nature of gravity. In this study, we examine the interferometer geometries proposed in these works, with particular attention to the commonly used approximation that neglects phase contributions from the vertical segments of the particle trajectories. Our analysis shows that this approximation can lead to incorrect predictions and, in certain parameter regimes, to null results where entanglement would otherwise be expected. We derive exact solutions that incorporate the full particle trajectories and demonstrate that the vertical arms can significantly affect the accumulated phase. Crucially, we identify configurations in which the induced entanglement vanishes entirely, a feature missed by simplified treatments. These findings show that accounting for the full interferometer geometry is not merely a refinement, but is essential for accurately assessing gravity-induced entanglement.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes interferometer geometries proposed for probing gravity-induced entanglement between massive particles, showing that the common approximation neglecting phase contributions from vertical trajectory segments leads to incorrect predictions—including null results where entanglement is expected, or vanishing entanglement where simplified treatments predict it. Exact solutions incorporating full particle trajectories demonstrate the vertical arms significantly affect accumulated phase, making full-geometry accounting essential.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the common simplification of neglecting vertical trajectory segments in proposed interferometer geometries for detecting gravity-induced entanglement yields correct predictions, or whether full geometric treatment is necessary for accurate assessment.
AI.method: The authors examine the interferometer geometries from prior proposals, identify the approximation that neglects phase contributions from vertical segments, derive exact solutions that incorporate full particle trajectories, and compare predictions across parameter regimes.
AI.result: The approximation neglecting vertical segment phases can lead to incorrect predictions and, in certain parameter regimes, null results where entanglement would otherwise be expected. The vertical arms significantly affect accumulated phase, and configurations exist where induced entanglement vanishes entirely—features missed by simplified treatments.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for the full interferometer geometry is essential, not merely a refinement, for accurately assessing gravity-induced entanglement in proposed quantum gravity experiments.

title: Emergent non-Markovianity in time-delayed waveguide QED
summary: Quantum systems are invariably coupled to a surrounding environment. A common theoretical method to simplify the problem is to trace over the environment under a Markov approximation, which assumes that the environment holds no memory over the timescales that the system evolves under. In interacting many-body systems, it is often not trivial to extract which of the multiple collective timescales are relevant. We consider a time-delayed waveguide QED setup with a single excitation. By fixing the maximum propagation time and increasing the number of emitters, we show that, even for small delay times, collective effects are sufficient to cause non-Markovianity. The impact of memory is intrinsically state-dependent. For superradiant states, the relevant system timescale is the superradiant lifetime while the relevant bath timescale is the end-to-end delay time. For subradiant states, both timescales depend on the structure of the specific state. Our results demonstrate the importance of prudently making Markov approximations in quantum many-body systems, and highlight potential pitfalls to avoid in scaling up quantum devices to large system sizes.

AI.tldr: This paper studies non-Markovianity in time-delayed waveguide QED systems with a single excitation, showing that collective effects among many emitters can induce non-Markovian behavior even for small delay times. The impact of memory is state-dependent: superradiant states set their timescale by the superradiant lifetime and end-to-end delay, while subradiant states have structure-dependent timescales. This highlights risks in applying Markov approximations to quantum many-body systems and scaling quantum devices.
AI.motivation: Markov approximations are commonly used to simplify quantum system-environment problems by tracing over the environment, assuming no memory. However, in interacting many-body systems, it is difficult to determine which collective timescales are relevant, and the validity of the Markov approximation is not obvious—especially as systems scale up.
AI.method: The authors consider a time-delayed waveguide QED setup with a single excitation. They fix the maximum propagation time and increase the number of emitters, then analyze non-Markovianity by examining the collective timescales of the system (e.g., superradiant vs. subradiant) against the bath timescale (end-to-end delay time).
AI.result: Even for small delay times, collective effects among many emitters are sufficient to cause non-Markovianity. For superradiant states, the relevant system timescale is the superradiant lifetime and the bath timescale is the end-to-end delay time. For subradiant states, both timescales depend on the structure of the specific state.
AI.conclusion: Markov approximations in quantum many-body systems must be made with caution, as collective effects can introduce non-Markovian memory even at small delay times. The state-dependent impact of memory highlights potential pitfalls when scaling up quantum devices to larger system sizes.

title: Detuning-robust Rydberg entangling gates from echoed pulses
summary: Rydberg-based two-qubit gate fidelities in neutral atom arrays are limited chiefly by laser intensity inhomogeneity and by detuning errors from frequency miscalibration, background-field drift, intermediate state light shift and Doppler shifts. Quantum optimal control can suppress the former, but no pulse can render a controlled-Z gate first-order insensitive to detuning. Here we show that this obstruction can be circumvented by designing Rydberg gate pulses with every leading-order detuning error relegated to single-qubit Z-rotations, which an echoed sequence removes. The resulting maximally-entangling ZZ gate has no leading-order response to arbitrary detunings on either atom, maintaining an infidelity below $10^{-3}$ much wider range of single-atom detunings than previous gate designs. We further show that a large fraction of residual error is dominated by population outside the computational subspace, which can be converted into heralded erasures. Our results significantly reduce the requirements on laser frequency stability and intensity homogeneity, field calibration and atomic temperature toward practical fault-tolerant quantum computing with neutral atoms.

AI.tldr: The authors design Rydberg gate pulses that eliminate leading-order sensitivity to detuning errors by relegating them to single-qubit Z-rotations (removed via echoed sequences), producing a maximally-entangling ZZ gate with infidelity below 10⁻³ over a wide range of detunings. Residual errors are largely erasure-convertible, relaxing requirements on laser stability, field calibration, and temperature for fault-tolerant neutral-atom quantum computing.
AI.motivation: Rydberg-based two-qubit gate fidelities in neutral atom arrays are limited by laser intensity inhomogeneity and detuning errors (frequency miscalibration, background-field drift, intermediate state light shift, Doppler shifts). While quantum optimal control can suppress intensity inhomogeneity, no pulse can make a controlled-Z gate first-order insensitive to detuning, creating an obstruction to high-fidelity gates.
AI.method: The authors circumvent this obstruction by designing Rydberg gate pulses such that every leading-order detuning error is confined to single-qubit Z-rotations, which can be eliminated via an echoed sequence. This yields a maximally-entangling ZZ gate with no leading-order response to arbitrary detunings on either atom.
AI.result: The ZZ gate maintains infidelity below 10⁻³ over a much wider range of single-atom detunings compared to previous gate designs. A large fraction of residual error is dominated by population leakage outside the computational subspace, which can be converted into heralded erasures.
AI.conclusion: The approach significantly reduces requirements on laser frequency stability, intensity homogeneity, field calibration, and atomic temperature, advancing practical fault-tolerant quantum computing with neutral atoms.

title: Demystifying Relativistic Quantum Collapse
summary: Non-relativistic objective collapse theories have been remarkably successful in addressing the conceptual problems of standard quantum mechanics. Despite substantial efforts, the project of extending them to the relativistic domain remains burdened by significant conceptual objections and technical challenges, often taken to cast doubt on the viability of the program as a whole. On the conceptual side, relativistic collapse theories have been claimed to face challenges involving tension between instantaneous collapse and relativity, frame-dependence of property values and probabilities, the possibility of superluminal signaling and the failure of narratability. On the technical side, persistent infinities, difficulties in constructing fully covariant frameworks and the apparent need for non-standard fields have hindered the development of workable models. In this paper, we offer a systematic rebuttal of the conceptual objections and provide a structured account of the remaining technical challenges. We conclude that relativistic collapse theories do provide a promising route toward a fully relativistic quantum framework that overcomes the conceptual limitations of standard quantum theory.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically rebuts conceptual objections to relativistic objective collapse theories and provides a structured account of remaining technical challenges, concluding that such theories offer a promising path toward a fully relativistic quantum framework.
AI.motivation: Non-relativistic objective collapse theories successfully address conceptual problems of standard quantum mechanics, but extending them to the relativistic domain faces significant skepticism due to conceptual objections and technical challenges that cast doubt on the entire program's viability.
AI.method: The paper offers a systematic rebuttal of conceptual objections (regarding instantaneous collapse vs. relativity, frame-dependence of properties and probabilities, superluminal signaling, and narratability) and provides a structured classification of the remaining technical challenges (persistent infinities, constructing fully covariant frameworks, and the need for non-standard fields).
AI.result: The conceptual objections are rebutted and the technical challenges are systematically structured, showing they are not fatal barriers.
AI.conclusion: Relativistic collapse theories provide a promising route toward a fully relativistic quantum framework that overcomes the conceptual limitations of standard quantum theory.

title: Strong Coupling of the Mo Mo Stretching Mode to a Locally Confined Stokes Raman Field in Mo2 Molecular Resonators
summary: Confining optical fields to molecular dimensions is a central objective in nanophotonics and molecular quantum optics. Here, we report strong coupling of the Mo Mo stretching vibration to a locally confined Raman scattering field in quadruply bonded dimolybdenum complexes. Under ambient, cavity-free conditions, the dimolybdenum formamidinate complexes Mo2(DAniF)4 and Mo2(DTolF)4 exhibit Rabi-type splitting, Mollow-type sidebands, and higher-order Raman features centered near the Mo Mo stretching frequency of 400 cm-1, indicating formation of dressed vibration field states. The sideband displacements from the resonance follow the photon-number-dependent relation Ωn=Ωνn, consistent with Jaynes Cummings-type coupling, while strongly displaced Raman features are assigned to leapfrog transitions within the same dressed-state ladder. In contrast, the less polarizable Mo2(O2CCH3)4 complex exhibits essentially a single Mo Mo stretching band. Reanalysis of reported resonance Raman spectra of an alkynyl Mo2 complex further supports this coupling framework. These results suggest that the Mo2 unit simultaneously serves as the Raman active oscillator and the molecular resonator that supports, confines, and enhances the locally generated scattering field, providing spectroscopic evidence for vibration field coupling and optical-field confinement within a chemically defined metal metal bond.

AI.tldr: This paper reports strong coupling between the Mo–Mo stretching vibration and a locally confined Raman scattering field in quadruply bonded dimolybdenum complexes, under ambient, cavity-free conditions. Evidence includes Rabi-type splitting, Mollow-type sidebands, and higher-order Raman features near 400 cm⁻¹, consistent with Jaynes-Cummings-type dressed-state coupling.
AI.motivation: The central objective is confining optical fields to molecular dimensions for applications in nanophotonics and molecular quantum optics, and achieving this in a chemically defined system without an external optical cavity.
AI.method: Raman spectroscopy of dimolybdenum formamidinate complexes (Mo2(DAniF)4, Mo2(DTolF)4) and comparison to the less polarizable Mo2(O2CCH3)4 complex; reanalysis of reported resonance Raman spectra of an alkynyl Mo2 complex.

The less polarizable acetate complex shows only a single Mo–Mo stretching band.
AI.conclusion: The Mo2 unit acts simultaneously as the Raman-active oscillator and the molecular resonator that supports, confines, and enhances the locally generated scattering field, providing spectroscopic evidence for vibration-field coupling and optical-field confinement within a chemically defined metal–metal bond.

title: Real-Space Analysis of Two-Photon Polarization States in Type-II SPDC for High-Purity Polarization Entanglement
summary: Spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) is one of the most widely used sources of polarization-entangled photon pairs, and understanding the generated biphoton state is essential for realizing high-brightness and high-purity entangled-photon sources. In particular, Type-II SPDC produces a biphoton wavefunction with a complex coupling between the spatial and polarization degrees of freedom owing to birefringence. In this study, we calculate the real-space distribution of the two-photon polarization state from the biphoton wavefunction of Type-II SPDC generated in a \b{eta}-barium borate (BBO) crystal. By identifying the spatial correlation direction between polarization and real-space coordinates, we designed aperture shapes that restrict the collection along this correlation direction. Through both numerical simulations and experiments, we demonstrate that such correlation-aligned apertures simultaneously achieve higher entanglement purity and improved photon collection efficiency. These results establish a practical design principle for optimizing aperture geometries based on the real-space biphoton wavefunction, providing a new approach to realizing high-purity and high-brightness SPDC entangled-photon sources.

AI.tldr: The authors analyze Type-II SPDC biphoton wavefunctions in BBO crystals, calculate the real-space polarization-state distribution, and demonstrate that correlation-aligned apertures (shaped to match the spatial-polarization coupling direction) simultaneously improve both entanglement purity and photon collection efficiency in entangled-photon sources.
AI.motivation: Type-II SPDC is a widely used source of polarization-entangled photon pairs, but the biphoton state exhibits complex spatial-polarization coupling due to birefringence. Understanding and mitigating this coupling is essential for realizing high-brightness and high-purity entangled-photon sources, yet conventional aperture designs do not account for the real-space correlation structure of the biphoton wavefunction.
AI.method: The authors calculate the real-space distribution of the two-photon polarization state from the Type-II SPDC biphoton wavefunction generated in a BBO crystal. They identify the spatial correlation direction between polarization and real-space coordinates, and design aperture shapes that restrict collection along this correlation direction. The approach is validated through both numerical simulations and experiments.
AI.result: The correlation-aligned apertures simultaneously achieve higher entanglement purity and improved photon collection efficiency compared to conventional aperture designs.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a practical design principle for optimizing aperture geometries based on the real-space biphoton wavefunction, providing a new approach to realizing high-purity and high-brightness SPDC entangled-photon sources.

title: Auditing Structured Randomness for Quantum Error Correction under a Bounded Cloud Fault Model
summary: Cloud quantum processors compile submitted quantum error correction circuits and may colocate them with untrusted workloads. A fixed public encoder gives a fault-injection adversary a reusable target. Per-run reseeding changes the physical-to-logical fault map. Exact Haar-random encoders have exponential circuit cost. Efficient random ensembles provide average-moment guarantees and leave worst-case accepted corruption uncharacterized. We define accepted logical disturbance, an acceptance-weighted measure of harmful logical action in accepted results, and derive its exact Haar expectation. We evaluate a polynomial-cost seeded Clifford encoder family using dense linear algebra and gate-level stabilizer simulation against faults chosen before or after the encoder is known. Reseeding reduces mean accepted logical disturbance from 0.150 for faults chosen after learning each encoder to 0.020 for one fault chosen before it is known. The 86.7% reduction results from rejection. The fixed distance-three \([[5,1,3]]\) code corrects every tested weight-one Pauli, while 18.5% of sampled encoders in the selected ensemble satisfy exact quantum error correction. The measured reduction quantifies the integrity gain from reseeding and separates postselected detection from exact correction under explicit fault and attacker-knowledge models.

It defines "accepted logical disturbance" as a measure of harmful logical action in accepted results, derives its exact Haar expectation, and evaluates a polynomial-cost seeded Clifford encoder family. Reseeding reduces mean accepted logical disturbance from 0.150 to 0.020 (86.7% reduction) under different attacker-knowledge models.
AI.motivation: Cloud quantum processors compile submitted quantum error correction circuits and may co-locate them with untrusted workloads, creating security vulnerabilities. A fixed public encoder gives fault-injection adversaries a reusable target. While exact Haar-random encoders would provide optimal security, they have exponential circuit cost, and efficient random ensembles only guarantee average-moment security while leaving worst-case accepted corruption uncharacterized.

They evaluate a polynomial-cost seeded Clifford encoder family using dense linear algebra and gate-level stabilizer simulation against two attacker scenarios: faults chosen after learning each encoder, and faults chosen before it is known.

The fixed distance-three [[5,1,3]] code corrects every tested weight-one Pauli, while only 18.5% of sampled encoders in the selected ensemble satisfy exact quantum error correction, separating postselected detection from exact correction.

title: Quantum-enhanced single and multiparameter metrology in qutrit ensembles by generalized twisting dynamics
summary: Quantum-enhanced sensing with atomic ensembles has predominantly focused on qubit-based protocols, despite the growing ability of many experimental platforms to coherently control and entangle multi-level systems. Here, we investigate quantum-enhanced sensing with qutrit ensembles by introducing three experimentally feasible qutrit generalisations of the one-axis twisting (OAT) model that involve entangling operations only between two levels, while the third level primarily acts as a spectator. We characterize the metrological utility of the dynamically generated states using the quantum Fisher information toolbox. We find numerically that all three models offer considerable freedom in encoding direction for quantum-enhanced sensing, with up to 6 out of 8 possible directions exhibit near-Heisenberg scaling after a short evolution time. We discuss experimental access to this enhanced metrological precision via effective time-reversal protocols. Furthermore, we examine the practical issues of estimation ambiguity and local dissipation, and show that they can be largely overcome by optimizing the sensor operating point. Finally, we show that the measurement incompatibility in estimating multiple parameters simultaneously encoded in different directions with near-Heisenberg scaling of precision is suppressed at the zero operating point as the system size increases. In the process, we find that one of the models enables near-Heisenberg scaling metrology with a pair of commuting generators, a possibility that arises from the $su(3)$ algebra and is thus absent in qubit-ensemble based sensors of collective $SU(2)$ rotations.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates quantum-enhanced sensing using qutrit (three-level) atomic ensembles, introducing three experimentally feasible generalizations of one-axis twisting (OAT) that entangle only two levels while the third acts as a spectator. Using quantum Fisher information, the authors find that all three models enable near-Heisenberg scaling in up to 6 of 8 encoding directions, discuss time-reversal-based readout, address estimation ambiguity and dissipation, and show that multi-parameter measurement incompatibility is suppressed at the zero operating point. Notably, one model achieves near-Heisenberg metrology with commuting generators—a possibility unique to su(3) algebra and absent in qubit-based sensors.
AI.motivation: Quantum-enhanced sensing with atomic ensembles has been predominantly limited to qubit-based protocols, despite the demonstrated experimental capability to control and entangle multi-level (qutrit) systems. The authors aim to expand the metrological toolbox by exploring whether qutrit ensembles can offer advantages over qubit-based one-axis twisting sensors, particularly in encoding flexibility and multi-parameter estimation.

They characterize the metrological performance of the dynamically generated states using the quantum Fisher information (QFI) toolbox, numerically analyzing encoding directions, Heisenberg scaling behavior, time-reversal protocols for experimental access, and practical issues including estimation ambiguity and local dissipation. They also analyze multi-parameter estimation and measurement incompatibility using the QFI matrix framework.
AI.result: All three qutrit OAT models allow considerable freedom in encoding direction, with up to 6 of 8 possible directions exhibiting near-Heisenberg scaling after short evolution. Effective time-reversal protocols provide experimental access to this precision. Estimation ambiguity and dissipation can be largely mitigated by optimizing the sensor operating point. The measurement incompatibility for multi-parameter estimation is suppressed at the zero operating point as system size grows. One model achieves near-Heisenberg metrology with commuting generators, enabled by su(3) algebra—a capability absent in qubit-based SU(2) collective rotation sensors.
AI.conclusion: Qutrit ensembles offer a richer metrological landscape than qubit-based sensors, providing more flexible encoding directions, multi-parameter estimation with suppressed incompatibility, and unique possibilities such as near-Heisenberg scaling with commuting generators arising from the su(3) algebra structure. These results establish qutrit OAT models as promising and feasible platforms for quantum-enhanced sensing.

title: Quantum estimation theory with quantum noise control
summary: Quantum estimation theory serves as one of fundamental backbones of quantum Shannon information theory and was mathematically systematized by pioneers of quantum information science. Although its applied research saw limited progress for a long period, the 21st century has witnessed active discussions and numerous fruitful proposals regarding its applications. Notably, the contributions of Monras and Paris represent one of the most remarkable achievements addressing the realization problem of estimation bounds. This paper aims to demonstrate a practical direction for extending their original ideas. Next-generation quantum information mechanisms urgently demand guarantees of quantum advantage unattainable by classical theory, alongside strict real-time processing without delays. By leveraging the concept of generalized heterodyne detection proposed nearly half a century ago, we demonstrate that a scheme based on their results can effectively meet the stringent requirements of near-future information technologies.

While recent contributions (notably by Monras and Paris) addressed the realization problem of estimation bounds, practical extensions are needed to meet the stringent demands of next-generation quantum information mechanisms, including guaranteed quantum advantage over classical methods and strict real-time processing without delays.

AI.conclusion: By combining the theoretical foundations of Monras and Paris with the long-standing concept of generalized heterodyne detection, the paper demonstrates a viable practical pathway for quantum estimation that can meet the demands of next-generation quantum information technologies, thereby expanding the applied scope of this foundational theory.

title: A thermometric quantum Brownian model for low-temperature electronics
summary: Quantum mechanical models of resistors in quantum electronics are often based on the quantum optical master equation (QOME). The QOME overlooks several fundamental properties, limiting its ability to model certain superconducting phenomena. Here we present a thermometric model of resistors, adapted from the quantum Brownian motion equation (QBME), that facilitates practical use of the QBME in modelling dissipative electronics at low temperatures. We compare the thermometric QBME presented here with predictions of the QOME, in the simple example of a transmon shunted by a resistor. We show that both the QBME and QOME yield comparable but physically distinct predictions, and discuss potential experimental tests with which to discriminate their use in modelling practical experiments.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a thermometric model of resistors based on the quantum Brownian motion equation (QBME), adapted for practical use in modeling dissipative electronics at low temperatures, and compares its predictions with the quantum optical master equation (QOME) using a transmon shunted by a resistor as an example.
AI.motivation: The quantum optical master equation (QOME), commonly used to model resistors in quantum electronics, overlooks several fundamental properties and thus limits its ability to model certain superconducting phenomena. A more accurate alternative, the QBME, has been available but lacked a practical thermometric formulation suitable for modeling dissipative electronics at low temperatures.
AI.method: The authors develop a thermometric model of resistors adapted from the QBME to make it practically applicable for modeling dissipative electronics at low temperatures. They then compare this thermometric QBME with the predictions of the QOME using the simple example of a transmon shunted by a resistor.
AI.result: Both the QBME and QOME yield comparable but physically distinct predictions for the transmon shunted by a resistor. The differences suggest potential experimental tests to discriminate which model is the appropriate one for modeling practical experiments.
AI.conclusion: The thermometric QBME provides a practical and more physically complete framework for modeling dissipative electronics at low temperatures than the QOME, with distinguishable experimental predictions that can be tested to determine the appropriate model for practical quantum electronics applications.

title: Adiabatic Otto-like quantum thermodynamical cycle in the non-quasi-static regime
summary: We show a finite-time Otto-like quantum thermodynamic cycle that preserves the adiabatic population structure of a time-dependent harmonic oscillator in the non-quasi-static regime. In the conventional energy representation, finite-rate driving induces non-adiabatic population redistribution and leaves residual excitations after the Hamiltonian has returned to its initial value. We show that this difficulty can be avoided by formulating the dynamics in the Lewis-Riesenfeld invariant representation, without modifying the physical Hamiltonian through auxiliary counterdiabatic driving. For a parametric Mathieu protocol, quantum inertia produces a mismatch between the spatial width of the working mode and its transient dressed energy scale. We propose an experimental implementation of this scheme in a trapped-ion Paul trap using stimulated Raman interactions, with independent control of the laser detuning and beam intersection angle. This provides a finite-time implementation in which the invariant population structure is preserved while the physical trap frequency evolves non-quasi-statically. Our results establish a clear distinction between adiabatic operation and quasi-static driving, providing a route toward finite-time quantum thermal cycles that retain the adiabatic energy structure without requiring the quasi-static limit.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a finite-time Otto-like quantum thermodynamic cycle that preserves the adiabatic population structure of a time-dependent harmonic oscillator outside the quasi-static regime, by formulating dynamics in the Lewis-Riesenfeld invariant representation rather than the conventional energy representation, without auxiliary counterdiabatic driving. An experimental implementation in a trapped-ion Paul trap using stimulated Raman interactions is proposed.
AI.motivation: Conventional finite-rate driving in quantum thermodynamic cycles induces non-adiabatic population redistribution and residual excitations when the Hamiltonian returns to its initial value, breaking the adiabatic energy structure that is typically only preserved in the quasi-static limit.
AI.method: The dynamics are reformulated in the Lewis-Riesenfeld invariant representation for a time-dependent harmonic oscillator, avoiding non-adiabatic transitions in the population structure without modifying the physical Hamiltonian. A parametric Mathieu protocol is used, and the scheme is realized in a trapped-ion Paul trap via stimulated Raman interactions with independent control of laser detuning and beam intersection angle.
AI.result: The invariant population structure is preserved while the physical trap frequency evolves non-quasi-statically, achieved in a finite-time implementation. Quantum inertia produces a mismatch between the spatial width of the working mode and its transient dressed energy scale for the parametric Mathieu protocol.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a clear distinction between adiabatic operation and quasi-static driving, providing a route toward finite-time quantum thermal cycles that retain the adiabatic energy structure without requiring the quasi-static limit.

title: Observing relativistic trajectories of single photons
summary: While the standard interpretation of quantum mechanics does not assign definite trajectories to particles, the Bohmian interpretation does.
