Only recently has an operational method for reconciling Bohmian mechanics with relativity been proposed. Here, we experimentally reconstruct relativistic Bohmian trajectories of a single photon in a Michelson-Sagnac interferometer, where counter-propagating probability amplitudes interfere head-on at the speed of light. As predicted by the relativistic Bohmian theory, we observe subluminal and superluminal features of the Bohmian trajectories of the photon traversing through the fringes. Our work provides experimental access to relativistic Bohmian mechanics and enables exploration of its unusual and counterintuitive properties.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally reconstructs relativistic Bohmian trajectories of a single photon in a Michelson-Sagnac interferometer, observing subluminal and superluminal features consistent with relativistic Bohmian theory predictions.
AI.motivation: While standard quantum mechanics does not assign definite particle trajectories, Bohmian mechanics does. However, reconciling Bohmian mechanics with relativity has been a longstanding challenge, and only recently an operational method for this reconciliation was proposed—motivating experimental verification.
AI.method: The experiment uses a Michelson-Sagnac interferometer where counter-propagating probability amplitudes interfere head-on at the speed of light. Relativistic Bohmian trajectories of a single photon are reconstructed using the recently proposed operational approach.
AI.result: The reconstructed trajectories exhibit both subluminal and superluminal features as predicted by relativistic Bohmian theory, confirming the theory's predictions experimentally.
AI.conclusion: The work provides experimental access to relativistic Bohmian mechanics, enabling further exploration of its unusual and counterintuitive properties.

title: Uncertainty limits for post-selected metrology
summary: For unitary transformations, the quantum Fisher information (QFI) of a pure state is given by the uncertainty of the generator in that state. In post-selected metrology, the QFI is given by a modified expression describing conditional quantum statistics of the generator. Here, we show that the conditional generator uncertainties defined by post-selected QFI correspond to Ozawa-Hall uncertainties known from the theoretical analysis of quantum measurements. The post-selected measurement outcome updates the generator uncertainty according to the quantum statistics of that outcome. Enhancements of QFI beyond the maximal uncertainties of the generator eigenvalues are possible because post-selection tends to concentrate the largest part of the initial generator uncertainty in low probability outcomes of the post-selection measurement. Anomalous conditional uncertainties thus explain the extreme sensitivities that can be achieved in post-selected metrology.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that the quantum Fisher information in post-selected metrology corresponds to Ozawa-Hall uncertainties, explaining how post-selection can enhance measurement sensitivity beyond the maximal uncertainty of generator eigenvalues by concentrating initial uncertainty into low-probability outcomes.
AI.motivation: To understand and explain the mechanism behind the extreme sensitivities achievable in post-selected metrology, particularly how conditional generator uncertainties can exceed the standard limits imposed by generator eigenvalues.
AI.method: The authors show that the modified expression for quantum Fisher information in post-selected metrology corresponds to Ozawa-Hall uncertainties from quantum measurement theory, and demonstrate that post-selection concentrates the largest part of the initial generator uncertainty into low-probability measurement outcomes.
AI.result: The study establishes that post-selected QFI enhancements beyond maximal generator eigenvalue uncertainties are possible because post-selection redistributes uncertainty into low-probability outcomes, giving rise to anomalous conditional uncertainties.
AI.conclusion: The anomalous conditional uncertainties identified as Ozawa-Hall uncertainties explain the extreme sensitivities achievable in post-selected metrology, providing a theoretical bridge between quantum measurement theory and post-selected quantum estimation.

title: Quantum Rare-Event Estimation for Ising Graphical Models with Belief-Propagation State Preparation
summary: Quantum amplitude estimation can reduce the sampling cost of rare-event probability estimation, but applying it to correlated Ising graphical models is limited by the difficulty of preparing the target distribution and building a practical event oracle. This work explores two approximate strategies for mitigating these challenges. We introduce a sample-free state-preparation method combining loopy belief propagation with the Chow--Liu algorithm. The resulting tree approximation is compiled into a quantum circuit with linear gate count and depth, and its accuracy is evaluated across graph families spanning different topologies, coupling strengths, and coupling signs. We also construct a structural oracle that evaluates threshold rules with reversible Boolean gates. Using a twenty-node supply-chain disruption model as a case study, we compare maximum likelihood amplitude estimation against four classical Monte Carlo baselines. Under the fixed-depth schedule used throughout this work, the quantum estimator has the same asymptotic error scaling as the classical methods but achieves lower estimation error by a constant factor. This reduction narrows when amplitude-encoding queries replace raw shots as the resource metric. We separate statistical error from the deterministic errors caused by approximate state preparation and oracle construction, and identify the requirements for achieving an improvement beyond a constant factor.

AI.tldr: This paper presents approximate quantum amplitude estimation techniques for rare-event probability estimation in correlated Ising graphical models, using a sample-free state-preparation method (combining loopy belief propagation with the Chow–Liu algorithm) and a structural oracle built from reversible Boolean gates. On a twenty-node supply-chain disruption model, the quantum estimator matches classical asymptotic error scaling but achieves lower constant-factor error, though this advantage narrows under certain resource metrics.
AI.motivation: Quantum amplitude estimation can reduce the sampling cost of rare-event probability estimation, but its application to correlated Ising models is obstructed by two key challenges: preparing the target distribution as a quantum state and constructing a practical event oracle. The authors aim to mitigate these difficulties with approximate strategies while assessing the practical quantum advantage.
AI.method: The authors introduce a sample-free state-preparation approach that combines loopy belief propagation with the Chow–Liu algorithm to produce a tree approximation, which is then compiled into a quantum circuit with linear gate count and depth. They also construct a structural oracle using reversible Boolean gates to evaluate threshold rules. The method is tested on a twenty-node supply-chain disruption model and compared against four classical Monte Carlo baselines under maximum likelihood amplitude estimation.
AI.result: Under a fixed-depth schedule, the quantum estimator achieves the same asymptotic error scaling as classical methods but with lower estimation error by a constant factor. This improvement narrows when amplitude-encoding queries replace raw shots as the resource metric. The authors separate statistical error from deterministic errors due to approximate state preparation and oracle construction.
AI.conclusion: The authors identify the requirements for achieving an improvement beyond a constant factor over classical Monte Carlo methods, clarifying the conditions under which quantum amplitude estimation provides meaningful practical advantages for rare-event probability estimation in Ising graphical models.

title: Energy Ordering from Nonlinear Quantum Dissipation
summary: Energy-ordered occupation is deeply embedded in quantum physics, from the Aufbau principle governing the filling of electronic states in atoms and molecules to the emergence of low-energy configurations in quantum many-body systems. However, the dynamical mechanism by which a generic quantum state develops such an energy hierarchy remains a fundamental question. Here we show that such an energy hierarchy can emerge dynamically from nonlinear quantum dissipation. Rather than being imposed as a principle or generated through coupling to a thermal reservoir, an Aufbau-like ordering of energy levels emerges intrinsically under quantum Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert dynamics from a generic initial mixed state. This convergence is a nontrivial consequence of Lyapunov monotonicity and instability of disordered population configurations. The resulting dynamics establish an intrinsic nonlinear mechanism for organizing density-matrix populations and provides a route toward selective preparation of low-energy subspaces. Numerical simulations confirm analytical predictions and illustrate convergence toward low-energy sectors.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that energy-ordered population occupation (Aufbau-like hierarchy) can emerge intrinsically from nonlinear quantum dissipation governed by quantum Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert dynamics, without requiring external thermal reservoirs or imposed ordering principles.
AI.motivation: Energy-ordered occupation is fundamental in quantum physics (e.g., the Aufbau principle), yet the dynamical mechanism by which a generic quantum state develops this energy hierarchy has remained an open question. The authors aim to explain this emergence dynamically.
AI.method: The authors analyze quantum Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert (qLLG) dynamics as a nonlinear dissipative evolution for density matrices. They establish that convergence to Aufbau-like ordering follows from Lyapunov monotonicity and the instability of disordered population configurations, and they support their analytical results with numerical simulations.
AI.result: Numerical simulations confirm the analytical predictions, illustrating that generic initial mixed states converge toward low-energy sectors under the nonlinear dissipative dynamics, driven by Lyapunov monotonicity and instability of disordered configurations.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes an intrinsic nonlinear mechanism for organizing density-matrix populations into energy-ordered hierarchies, offering a route toward selective preparation of low-energy subspaces without relying on external thermal reservoirs.

title: Bound-state-mediated remote charging of a quantum battery
summary: Remote charging of a quantum battery (QB) is hindered by radiative leakage of the excitation into the photonic environment that acts as a mediator for energy transfer. We consider a charger-battery model consisting of two two-level systems (TLSs) that are locally coupled to two sites of a one-dimensional coupled cavity array. When their transition frequency lies outside the propagation band, the system forms atom-photon bound states with localized photonic components, and the overlap of these components lifts the degeneracy of the even- and odd-parity bound states, yielding an energy splitting that drives coherent energy transfer from the charger to the QB. In this way, the band gap suppresses resonant emission and the localized bound states mediate remote charging. From the parity-resolved spectrum, we relate the charging time to the energy splitting and the charged ergotropy to the fraction of TLS population on the bound states. Bound states closer to the band edge extend the interaction range of the TLSs but contain a large photonic fraction and are consequently more susceptible to photon loss.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates remote charging of a quantum battery in a one-dimensional coupled cavity array, where two two-level systems (charger and battery) are coupled to separate cavity sites. When the TLS transition frequency lies outside the propagation band, atom-photon bound states form and their overlap lifts the degeneracy between even- and odd-parity states, creating an energy splitting that drives coherent energy transfer and enables remote charging while suppressing radiative losses. The charging time is related to the energy splitting, and the charged ergotropy depends on the fraction of TLS population in the bound states, with bound states near the band edge offering longer interaction ranges but higher susceptibility to photon loss.
AI.motivation: Remote charging of quantum batteries is a desirable capability, but it is fundamentally limited by radiative leakage of excitation into the photonic environment used as the energy-transfer mediator. The authors aim to overcome this obstacle by exploiting atom-photon bound states to mediate coherent, loss-suppressed remote energy transfer.
AI.method: The model consists of a charger-battery system built from two two-level systems locally coupled to two sites of a one-dimensional coupled cavity array. The TLS transition frequency is tuned outside the propagation band so that atom-photon bound states form with localized photonic components. By analyzing the parity-resolved spectrum, the authors derive the energy splitting between even- and odd-parity bound states, relate it to the charging time, and connect the charged ergotropy to the TLS population fraction residing on the bound states.
AI.result: The band gap suppresses resonant emission while the localized bound states mediate remote charging. The charging time is directly linked to the energy splitting of the parity-resolved bound states, and the charged ergotropy is determined by the fraction of TLS population occupying bound states. Bound states closer to the band edge extend the TLS interaction range but contain a larger photonic fraction, making them more vulnerable to photon loss.
AI.conclusion: The proposed scheme demonstrates that photonic band-gap engineering can enable efficient remote charging of quantum batteries via delocalized atom-photon bound states, with a tunable trade-off between interaction range, charging speed, and robustness against photon loss.

title: Quantum Interconnects Part I: Strategic Quantum Network Formation
summary: The realization of large-scale quantum networks requires more than advances in quantum repeaters, memories, and processors, it requires a framework explaining how heterogeneous quantum technologies evolve from isolated deployments into interconnected infrastructures. While the classical Internet evolved under strong utility incentives associated with resource sharing and communication demands, quantum networking currently lacks dominant applications capable of generating comparable incentives. As a consequence, contemporary quantum networks are largely formed through technology-driven decisions motivated by technical feasibility, experimental validation, and expected future value. This work argues that the absence of utility-driven network formation is not solely a consequence of immature applications, but also of insufficient abstraction. In particular, heterogeneous quantum platforms remain tightly coupled to the functionalities they provide, preventing the definition of technology-independent utility functions. A hierarchical architecture consisting of Physical Platforms (PP), Functionalities (F), Services (S), Applications (A), and Use-Cases (UC) is proposed, together with the argument that quantum interconnects constitute the enabling technology required to decouple physical implementations from network functionalities. Such decoupling permits the definition of utility functions at the functionality level and establishes the conditions under which strategic (agent-based) network formation becomes applicable. Quantum interconnects should therefore be viewed not only as interoperability devices, but also as fundamental enablers of strategic quantum network evolution.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that large-scale quantum networks lack utility-driven formation due to insufficient abstraction—heterogeneous quantum platforms are tightly coupled to their functionalities. It proposes a hierarchical architecture (Physical Platforms, Functionalities, Services, Applications, Use-Cases) where quantum interconnects serve as the enabling technology to decouple physical implementations from network functionalities, thereby making strategic, agent-based network formation possible.
AI.motivation: Large-scale quantum networks require a framework for how heterogeneous quantum technologies evolve from isolated deployments into interconnected infrastructures. Unlike the classical Internet, which grew under utility incentives, quantum networking lacks dominant applications generating comparable incentives, leading to technology-driven (rather than utility-driven) network formation. The authors argue this is partly due to insufficient abstraction—not just immature applications.
AI.method: The paper proposes a conceptual hierarchical architecture comprising Physical Platforms (PP), Functionalities (F), Services (S), Applications (A), and Use-Cases (UC). It argues that quantum interconnects are the key enabling technology to decouple physical implementations from network functionalities, allowing utility functions to be defined at the functionality level and enabling strategic (agent-based) network formation.
AI.result: The proposed architecture demonstrates that decoupling physical platforms from functionalities via quantum interconnects permits utility function definitions at the functionality level, establishing conditions under which strategic agent-based network formation becomes applicable to quantum networks.
AI.conclusion: Quantum interconnects should be viewed not merely as interoperability devices but as fundamental enablers of strategic quantum network evolution, providing the abstraction necessary for utility-driven network formation analogous to the classical Internet's development.

title: Correcting Connectivity in Arc-Based QUBO Models for Fixed-Fleet Vehicle Routing
summary: We revisit a degree-only arc Hamiltonian for fixed-fleet, homogeneous, uncapacitated vehicle routing. Because its local penalties define only a cycle cover, ground states may contain customer cycles disconnected from the depot. We construct a polynomial-size quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) repair using capped single-commodity flow and prove that every ground-state routing is connected and cost-optimal under explicit penalty assumptions. For $N-1$ customers and $K$ nonempty routes, the unreduced encoding uses exactly $|E|(1+\lceil\log_2(N-K+1)\rceil)$ logical problem qubits. A reversible compute--phase--uncompute realization evaluates the flow penalties in $O(N^2\log N+N\log^2N)$ logical gates on a complete graph with $O(\log N)$ reusable workspace and no product register. On complete loopless graphs, a depot-delimited single-sequence position encoding uses fewer problem qubits and fewer written terms when the flow-word length grows. Conversely, the flow model achieves a smaller structured logical-gate upper bound under a common reversible accounting model. Exact audits of the Hamiltonian and circuit implementation, combined with a $1{,}200$-matrix classical benchmark, verify the formulation and quantify the connectivity gap. Finally, a 32,000-shot Amazon Braket task on IQM Emerald characterizes depth-one termwise Ising circuits on a diagnostic $N = 4,\, K = 1$ counterexample instance. In the degree-only circuit, $78.05\%$ of selected $p=1$ shots realize the invalid disconnected ground state; the reduced 14-qubit flow-augmented circuit yields no fully feasible sample. These device results characterize mapped Hamiltonians and compilation rather than an asymptotic routing solution advantage.

AI.tldr: The paper revisits a degree-only Hamiltonian for vehicle routing and constructs a polynomial-size QUBO repair using capped single-commodity flow to guarantee connected, cost-optimal ground states, with detailed encoding sizes, gate counts, and device validation on IBM and IQM hardware.
AI.motivation: A degree-only arc Hamiltonian for vehicle routing defines only a cycle cover via local penalties, so ground states can contain customer cycles disconnected from the depot. This connectivity gap must be repaired to obtain valid routing solutions.
AI.method: The authors construct a polynomial-size QUBO repair using capped single-commodity flow and prove connectedness and cost-optimality of ground states under explicit penalty assumptions. They detail the unreduced encoding size (|E|(1+ceil(log2(N-K+1))) qubits), a reversible compute-phase-uncompute circuit with O(N^2 log N + N log^2 N) gates and O(log N) workspace, compare a depot-delimited single-sequence position encoding, and validate via exact audits, a 1,200-matrix classical benchmark, and a 32,000-shot quantum task on IQM Emerald.
AI.result: The degree-only circuit yields 78.05% of selected p=1 shots realizing an invalid disconnected ground state on a diagnostic N=4, K=1 counterexample, while the reduced 14-qubit flow-augmented circuit yields no fully feasible sample. The flow model achieves a smaller structured logical-gate upper bound than position encoding, though it uses more qubits/terms when flow-word length grows.
AI.conclusion: The flow-augmented repair formally guarantees connected, cost-optimal ground states, but device results on IQM Emerald characterize mapped Hamiltonians and compilation rather than demonstrating an asymptotic routing solution advantage.

title: Geometric optimality of entanglement-induced fast qubit reset
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures (main text and bibliography: 11 pages, 4 figures; appendices: 6 pages, 1 figure). Comments are welcome!
summary: Fast and reliable qubit reset is essential for the efficient operation of quantum processors. Among the proposed strategies, Mpemba-effect-based protocols offer a simple route to accelerated relaxation, but provide limited insight into the optimality of the full reset dynamics. Geometric approaches, by contrast, quantify optimality but do not generally suggest practical acceleration protocols. Here, we bridge these perspectives through a geometric analysis of entanglement-assisted qubit reset. We show that entangling operations can redistribute local coherences across a multi-qubit register, allowing the reduced state of each qubit to follow a geodesic path towards the ground state. Remarkably, this locally optimal behaviour can emerge even when the collective evolution becomes suboptimal in the full state space. We illustrate this interplay for different families of initial multi-qubit states. Our results provide a geometric perspective on Mpemba-inspired reset acceleration and clarify when extending two-qubit protocols to larger registers provides a further advantage in the reset process.

AI.tldr: The paper bridges geometric optimality analysis with Mpemba-effect-based protocols for qubit reset, showing that entangling operations enable local qubit states to follow geodesic (optimal) paths toward the ground state, even when the collective multi-qubit evolution is suboptimal in full state space.
AI.motivation: Fast and reliable qubit reset is critical for quantum processor efficiency. Mpemba-effect-based protocols offer simple acceleration but lack insight into optimality of the full reset dynamics, while geometric approaches quantify optimality but don't suggest practical acceleration protocols. The paper aims to bridge these two perspectives.
AI.method: The authors perform a geometric analysis of entanglement-assisted qubit reset, examining how entangling operations redistribute local coherences across a multi-qubit register. They analyze whether the reduced state of each qubit follows a geodesic path toward the ground state and test this for different families of initial multi-qubit states.
AI.result: Entangling operations allow local qubit coherences to be redistributed, enabling each qubit's reduced state to follow a geodesic (locally optimal) path to the ground state. This locally optimal behavior can emerge even when the collective evolution becomes suboptimal in the full state space. The authors illustrate this for various families of initial multi-qubit states.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a geometric perspective on Mpemba-inspired reset acceleration and clarify conditions under which extending two-qubit protocols to larger registers provides a further advantage in qubit reset processes.

title: Corrections induced by the GUP to the Lamb shift of an accelerated atom interacting with a quantum scalar field
summary: We investigate the effect of the GUP on the Lamb shift of a two-level atom interacting with a real massless scalar quantum field, within the DDC formalism. For an atom undergoing inertial motion, uniform acceleration, and uniform circular motion, we analyze the separate contributions of vacuum fluctuations and radiation reaction. We first derive the statistical functions of the field along the atom's trajectories for the three types of motion, expressing them as frequency integrals, and then employ them to calculate the vacuum fluctuation and radiation reaction contributions to the radiative level shift. We show that the GUP-modified Lamb shift of the two-level atom arises entirely from vacuum fluctuations and acquires additional corrections proportional to $β$. We focus in particular on the acceleration-dependent GUP corrections. For a uniformly accelerated atom, the GUP corrections comprise thermal and nonthermal parts. At low accelerations, the thermal part exhibits nonmonotonic behavior, and is proportional to $a^4$ in the limit $a/ω_0 \to 0$; the nonthermal part, by contrast, grows nonlinearly and monotonically, exceeding the thermal part by nearly two orders of magnitude at large accelerations. For an atom in uniform circular motion, the GUP corrections are purely nonthermal and also display a nonlinear, monotonic dependence on acceleration, increasing or decreasing steeply according to the sign of $β$. For the same $β$, the corrections are larger in uniform circular motion than in uniformly accelerated motion, since the former involves terms proportional to both $a^2$ and $a^3$, whereas the latter contains only $a^2$ terms.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the effects of the Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP) on the Lamb shift of a two-level atom interacting with a massless scalar quantum field, using the DDC (Dalibard, Dupont-Roc, Cohen-Tannoudji) formalism. The study examines three types of atomic motion—inertial, uniformly accelerated, and uniform circular—and shows that GUP-modified corrections arise entirely from vacuum fluctuations, scaling with the GUP parameter β. For accelerated motion, corrections include thermal and nonthermal parts with distinct behaviors; for circular motion, corrections are purely nonthermal and larger than in accelerated motion due to higher-order terms in acceleration.
AI.motivation: To understand how quantum gravity effects, encoded via the Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP), modify the Lamb shift of atoms in different states of motion within the framework of open quantum systems (DDC formalism).
AI.method: The authors use the DDC formalism to compute the separate contributions of vacuum fluctuations and radiation reaction to the radiative level shift. They derive the statistical (Wightman and Hadamard) functions of the scalar field along the three trajectories, express them as frequency integrals, and compute the GUP-modified radiative level shifts.
AI.result: The GUP-modified Lamb shift arises entirely from vacuum fluctuations with additional corrections proportional to β. For uniformly accelerated motion, corrections split into thermal and nonthermal parts: the thermal part is nonmonotonic at low accelerations, proportional to a⁴ as a/ω₀→0; the nonthermal part grows monotonically and nonlinearly, exceeding the thermal part by ~two orders of magnitude at high accelerations. For uniform circular motion, corrections are purely nonthermal and monotonic, increasing/decreasing steeply with the sign of β. For the same β, circular motion corrections are larger because they involve both a² and a³ terms, whereas accelerated motion contains only a² terms.
AI.conclusion: GUP modifies the Lamb shift of moving atoms through vacuum fluctuations, with characteristic acceleration-dependent corrections that distinguish between different types of motion. The scaling and sign behavior depend sensitively on the GUP parameter β and the atom's trajectory.

title: Cavity-assisted homodyne detection with a single photodiode
summary: High-frequency squeezed states are important for quantum metrology and information processing, but quadrature measurements at gigahertz frequencies remain challenging. Balanced homodyne detection (BHD), the standard approach, requires closely matched complex transfer functions in both photodetection channels to suppress local-oscillator (LO) noise and maintain a well-defined readout quadrature. This matching becomes increasingly difficult at high bandwidths. Strongly asymmetric single-photodiode homodyne detection avoids this requirement, but achieving high signal efficiency and shot-noise clearance typically requires hundreds of milliwatts of LO power and does not suppress technical LO sidebands. I propose cavity-assisted homodyne detection, in which the quantum field and LO enter separate ports of an impedance-matched traveling-wave cavity. The resonant LO carrier is transmitted to the photodetector, where it beats with off-resonant signal sidebands reflected from the cavity. At the same time, technical LO sidebands outside the cavity linewidth are suppressed. I derive the quantum input-output relations and linearized photocurrent including intracavity loss, and show that near-unity signal-transfer efficiency can be achieved at moderate incident LO power. The cavity linewidth and free spectral range determine the usable detection band.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes cavity-assisted homodyne detection as an alternative to balanced homodyne detection for measuring high-frequency squeezed states in the gigahertz band. By routing the quantum field and local oscillator through separate ports of an impedance-matched traveling-wave cavity, the scheme suppresses technical LO sidebands, achieves near-unity signal-transfer efficiency at moderate LO power, and avoids the stringent channel-matching requirements of BHD.
AI.motivation: Frequency squeezing at gigahertz frequencies is important for quantum metrology and information processing, but quadrature measurements at such high frequencies remain challenging. Balanced homodyne detection requires closely matched complex transfer functions between two photodetection channels, which becomes increasingly difficult at high bandwidths and limits LO noise suppression and readout-quadrature definition.
AI.method: The author proposes cavity-assisted homodyne detection: quantum field and LO enter separate ports of an impedance-matched traveling-wave cavity. The resonant LO carrier transmits to the photodetector and beats with off-resonant signal sidebands reflected from the cavity, while technical LO sidebands outside the cavity linewidth are suppressed. Quantum input-output relations and linearized photocurrent are derived including intracavity loss.
AI.result: The analysis shows that near-unity signal-transfer efficiency can be achieved at moderate incident LO power, overcoming the need for hundreds of milliwatts required by strongly asymmetric single-photodiode homodyne detection. The cavity linewidth and free spectral range set the usable detection bandwidth.
AI.conclusion: Cavity-assisted homodyne detection offers a practical route to high-efficiency, shot-noise-limited quadrature measurements at gigahertz frequencies without requiring closely matched detectors or high LO powers, while additionally rejecting technical LO sidebands.

title: Isotropic Nanoscale Quantum Sensor at Room-Temperature
summary: Color-center based quantum sensors provide nanoscale resolution under ambient conditions, yet their applicability remains limited. Because the quantization axes are locked to the host lattice, conventional color centers suffer severe signal loss in off-axis magnetic fields. To address this, we report an isotropic magnetometer enabled by the neutrally charged nitrogen-vacancy center (NV0) in diamond. Here, spin-to-charge dynamics yield an NV0-dark spin pair whose quantization axis dynamically aligns with the external field. Read out through NV charge-state-selective fluorescence, this system exhibits microsecond room-temperature coherence and nanotesla sensitivity for arbitrary field directions. We demonstrate alignment-free mapping of steep field gradients and single paramagnetic micro-targets, alongside isotropic readout from randomly oriented nanodiamonds. Resolving longstanding orientation constraints, this platform unlocks unrestricted nanoscale magnetometry across life sciences and quantum materials.

AI.tldr: This paper reports an isotropic diamond magnetometer based on the neutrally charged nitrogen-vacancy center (NV0). Unlike conventional color centers whose quantization axes are fixed to the host lattice, NV0's spin-to-charge dynamics generate a dark spin pair whose quantization axis dynamically aligns with the external magnetic field, enabling orientation-independent nanoscale magnetometry with microsecond room-temperature coherence, nanotesla sensitivity, and arbitrary-direction field mapping.
AI.motivation: Conventional color-center quantum sensors achieve nanoscale resolution under ambient conditions, but their quantization axes are locked to the host lattice, causing severe signal loss when operating in off-axis magnetic fields. This orientation constraint fundamentally limits their applicability in realistic settings where field directions are arbitrary or unknown.
AI.method: The authors utilize the neutrally charged nitrogen-vacancy center (NV0) in diamond. Through spin-to-charge conversion dynamics, an NV0-dark spin pair is created whose quantization axis dynamically reorients to align with the external magnetic field. Readout is performed via NV charge-state-selective fluorescence, leveraging the distinct optical properties of different charge states.
AI.result: The NV0-based magnetometer achieves microsecond room-temperature coherence times and nanotesla sensitivity for arbitrary magnetic field directions. It demonstrates alignment-free mapping of steep field gradients and single paramagnetic micro-targets, as well as isotropic readout from randomly oriented nanodiamonds.
AI.conclusion: The system resolves the longstanding orientation constraints of conventional color-center sensors by providing a fully isotropic magnetometry platform. This unlocks unrestricted nanoscale magnetic sensing across applications in life sciences and quantum materials research.

title: Quantum-enhanced ghost imaging recognition via joint optimization of speckle patterns and quantum network parameters
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, submitted to Physical Review A
summary: Ghost imaging enables nonlocal image reconstruction and exhibits strong robustness against interference, but achieving high-fidelity recognition at ultra-low sampling rates remains challenging. Quantum machine learning offers a novel approach for efficient feature extraction on noisy medium-scale quantum devices; however, existing methods generally suffer from low recognition accuracy and weak noise resistance. This paper proposes a ghost imaging recognition method based on the simultaneous optimization of speckle patterns and quantum network parameters. By leveraging the mathematical equivalence between classical convolution and speckle-object dot product operations in ghost imaging, a speckle consistency regularization mechanism is introduced to achieve end-to-end joint optimization of optical coding and quantum feature extractors. A parallel 8-qubit quantum circuit employing block coding and a star-shaped entanglement structure is designed to extract higher-order features from bucket signals. Simulation results on the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets show that at an ultra-low sampling rate of 1.5625%, the proposed framework achieves recognition accuracies of 90.1% and 81.7%, respectively, representing a 2.6% improvement over classical convolutional neural networks and a maximum improvement of 14.2% over traditional hybrid quantum machine learning models. This method also exhibits strong robustness to quantum noise and has been validated on a real optical ghost imaging system, achieving an average recognition accuracy of 84.8%. These results confirm that the joint optimization of speckle patterns and quantum network parameters provides a reliable and practical solution for low-sampling ghost imaging recognition.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a ghost imaging recognition method that jointly optimizes speckle patterns and quantum network parameters, using a parallel 8-qubit quantum circuit with block coding and star-shaped entanglement. At an ultra-low sampling rate of 1.5625%, it achieves 90.1% and 81.7% recognition accuracy on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST respectively, improving 2.6% over classical CNNs and up to 14.2% over traditional hybrid quantum models, with strong noise robustness validated on a real optical system (84.8% accuracy).
AI.motivation: Ghost imaging enables nonlocal image reconstruction with strong interference robustness, but high-fidelity recognition at ultra-low sampling rates remains challenging. Quantum machine learning offers efficient feature extraction on noisy quantum devices, yet existing methods suffer from low recognition accuracy and weak noise resistance. The paper aims to address both limitations simultaneously.
AI.method: The method leverages the mathematical equivalence between classical convolution and speckle-object dot product operations in ghost imaging to introduce a speckle consistency regularization mechanism, enabling end-to-end joint optimization of optical coding and quantum feature extractors. A parallel 8-qubit quantum circuit employing block coding and a star-shaped entanglement structure extracts higher-order features from bucket signals.
AI.result: On MNIST and Fashion-MNIST at 1.5625% sampling rate, the framework achieves 90.1% and 81.7% accuracy, improving 2.6% over classical CNNs and up to 14.2% over traditional hybrid quantum machine learning models. Strong robustness to quantum noise is demonstrated, and validation on a real optical ghost imaging system achieves 84.8% average recognition accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Joint optimization of speckle patterns and quantum network parameters provides a reliable and practical solution for low-sampling ghost imaging recognition, confirming the feasibility of integrating quantum feature extraction with optical coding in real-world systems.

title: A Superconducting Phase Transition Single-Electron Transistor
summary: Quantum computers require fast and accurate methods for qubit state detection. Phase-transition sensors exploit the abrupt change between two physical states of a material to achieve enhanced sensitivity and have enabled advanced detectors for quantum technologies, such as superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors. However, this sensing principle has not yet been applied to semiconductor spin qubits. Here, we demonstrate a superconducting phase-transition radio-frequency single-electron transistor (PTSET), a charge sensor for semiconductor spin qubits whose response is enhanced by a superconducting-to-normal phase transition. The transition is engineered by linking the sensor current to a low-critical-current, high-kinetic-inductance inductor integrated into the radio-frequency matching network. We demonstrate improvements in sensitivity of one and two orders of magnitude over conventional rfSETs in the large- and small-signal regimes, respectively. Our results establish phase-transition sensing as a route towards ultrasensitive, integrated charge sensors for semiconductor quantum computing and point to broader applications, including cryogenic photon detection for radio astronomy.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a superconducting phase-transition radio-frequency single-electron transistor (PTSET) as a charge sensor for semiconductor spin qubits, achieving one to two orders of magnitude sensitivity improvement over conventional rfSETs by exploiting a superconducting-to-normal phase transition engineered through a low-critical-current, high-kinetic-inductance inductor in the RF matching network.
AI.motivation: Quantum computers require fast and accurate qubit state detection. While phase-transition sensors have enabled advanced detectors like superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors, this sensing principle had not yet been applied to semiconductor spin qubits, leaving a gap in ultrasensitive charge sensing for these systems.
AI.method: The authors engineer a superconducting-to-normal phase transition in a radio-frequency single-electron transistor (PTSET) by linking the sensor current to a low-critical-current, high-kinetic-inductance inductor integrated into the RF matching network, thereby coupling the sensor response to the abrupt phase transition for enhanced detection sensitivity.
AI.result: The PTSET demonstrates sensitivity improvements of one order of magnitude over conventional rfSETs in the large-signal regime and two orders of magnitude in the small-signal regime.
AI.conclusion: Phase-transition sensing is established as a viable route toward ultrasensitive, integrated charge sensors for semiconductor quantum computing, with broader applications including cryogenic photon detection for radio astronomy.

title: Fast On-Chip Thermometry with TiN Kinetic Inductance Resonators in 22 nm Process Technology
summary: Understanding the temporal and spatial dependence of temperature is critical in high-performance cryogenic devices. Typical thermometry techniques struggle to simultaneously combine high bandwidth, sensitivity and on-chip integration, limiting their ability to measure fast intra-device thermal fluctuations. Here, we demonstrate a time-resolved thermometry platform based on TiN kinetic inductance resonators integrated in a 22 nm FDSOI chip. By tracking temperature-dependent shifts in the resonant frequency, we achieve sub-millikelvin temperature sensitivity down to temperatures of 100 mK. Time-resolved on-chip pulsed heating experiments as a function of distance reveal an onset delay, consistent with a quasi-ballistic heat propagation velocity of 3.9 ${\pm}$ 0.1 mm $μ$s${}^{-1}$. We also show that elevated temperatures increase net thermal conductance, shortening thermal relaxation times across all spatial separations. This behaviour manifests in two distinct regimes: a substrate-limited regime at 100 mK, where cooling rates vary with heater distance, and a Kapitza boundary-limited regime at 400 mK, where thermal relaxation becomes more spatially uniform.These measurements demonstrate kinetic inductance thermometry's ability to rapidly probe non-equilibrium temperature dynamics in cryogenic devices such as quantum processors.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a time-resolved thermometry platform using TiN kinetic inductance resonators integrated into a 22 nm FDSOI chip, achieving sub-millikelvin sensitivity at 100 mK and revealing quasi-ballistic heat propagation (3.9 mm/μs) and distance-dependent thermal relaxation dynamics governed by substrate-limited and Kapitza boundary-limited regimes.
AI.motivation: Typical cryogenic thermometry techniques cannot simultaneously achieve high bandwidth, sensitivity, and on-chip integration, which limits their ability to measure fast intra-device thermal fluctuations in high-performance cryogenic devices.
AI.method: TiN kinetic inductance resonators were integrated into a 22 nm FDSOI chip. Temperature-dependent resonant frequency shifts were tracked to measure temperature, and time-resolved on-chip pulsed heating experiments were performed as a function of distance to probe thermal dynamics.
AI.result: Sub-millikelvin temperature sensitivity was achieved down to 100 mK. Pulsed heating revealed an onset delay consistent with a quasi-ballistic heat propagation velocity of 3.9 ± 0.1 mm/μs. Elevated temperatures increased net thermal conductance, shortening thermal relaxation times. Two regimes were identified: substrate-limited at 100 mK (cooling rates vary with heater distance) and Kapitza boundary-limited at 400 mK (spatially uniform relaxation).
AI.conclusion: Kinetic inductance thermometry can rapidly probe non-equilibrium temperature dynamics in cryogenic devices, offering a path toward high-bandwidth thermal characterization of quantum processors.

title: Towards Reproducible Evaluation of Distributed Quantum Circuit Partitioning Algorithms
comment: Accepted at IEEE QCE 2026 Workshop: Distributed Quantum Computing Systems and Infrastructure
summary: Distributed Quantum Computing (DQC) addresses the physical scaling limitations of monolithic quantum processors by networking modular Quantum Processing Units (QPUs). Efficient execution of quantum algorithms on DQC architectures requires compiling them across QPUs while minimizing inter-QPU communication bottlenecks, primarily through circuit partitioning. However, current evaluations of state-of-the-art partitioning heuristics focus primarily on the total entanglement cost of the partitions, failing to capture the broader structural and temporal overheads introduced by distributed network constraints. This paper addresses this evaluation gap by applying established monolithic benchmarking metrics to partitioned distributed circuits to quantify the performance impact of network constraints. Using an open-source, automated evaluation pipeline, we systematically assess diverse partitioning algorithms across standardized workloads and quantum network topologies. Our empirical results reveal that partitioning algorithms with comparable entanglement costs can still introduce drastically different physical execution penalties. By exposing these hidden trade-offs, such as severe increases in circuit depth and substantial reductions in gate density, this study demonstrates that comprehensive circuit-level metrics are essential for guiding the future design of DQC compilers.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the evaluation gap in Distributed Quantum Computing (DQC) partitioning heuristics by applying established monolithic benchmarking metrics to partitioned distributed circuits, revealing that algorithms with comparable entanglement costs can introduce drastically different physical execution penalties such as increased circuit depth and reduced gate density.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of state-of-the-art partitioning heuristics in DQC focus primarily on total entanglement cost, failing to capture broader structural and temporal overheads introduced by distributed network constraints. This evaluation gap prevents a comprehensive understanding of how partitioning choices impact physical execution performance.
AI.method: The authors apply established monolithic benchmarking metrics to partitioned distributed circuits and use an open-source, automated evaluation pipeline to systematically assess diverse partitioning algorithms across standardized workloads and quantum network topologies.
AI.result: Empirical results show that partitioning algorithms with comparable entanglement costs can still introduce drastically different physical execution penalties, including severe increases in circuit depth and substantial reductions in gate density.
AI.conclusion: Comprehensive circuit-level metrics are essential for guiding the future design of DQC compilers, as hidden trade-offs exposed by these benchmarks are not captured by entanglement cost alone.

title: Kramers pseudospin and the quantum number proposed for the many-electron Dirac?Coulomb Hamiltonian
summary: The square of a sum of single-electron time reversals has been proposed as a conserved quantity with an integer eigenvalue spectrum for the many-electron Dirac-Coulomb Hamiltonian [Phys. Rev. A 94, 052104 (2016)], and its expectation value is in use as a diagnostic of Kramers contamination. This work identifies the operator behind the construction, a component of a pseudospin attached to the chosen Kramers pairs, whose angular-momentum algebra reproduces the reported spectrum and yields the eigenvectors in closed form. The label $k$ entering the proposed quantum number $-k^2$ is twice the magnitude of a pseudospin projection onto an axis fixed by the basis and changes when the Kramers pairs are rephased. The commutation with the Hamiltonian is unfounded, and the proposed quantum number does not stand.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies the operator behind a proposed conserved quantity for the many-electron Dirac-Coulomb Hamiltonian, showing it is a pseudospin component whose angular-momentum algebra explains the reported spectrum but whose commutation with the Hamiltonian is unfounded.
AI.motivation: A previously proposed quantum number, derived from the square of a sum of single-electron time reversals, has been used as a diagnostic of Kramers contamination. This work aims to identify the actual operator behind this construction and verify whether the proposed conservation law is valid.
AI.method: The authors identify the operator as a component of a pseudospin associated with the chosen Kramers pairs. They analyze the angular-momentum algebra of this operator to reproduce the reported integer eigenvalue spectrum and derive closed-form eigenvectors. They also examine how the label k varies with rephasing of Kramers pairs and test the claimed commutation with the Hamiltonian.
AI.result: The operator is identified as a pseudospin component whose angular-momentum algebra reproduces the reported spectrum with closed-form eigenvectors. The label k is twice the magnitude of a pseudospin projection onto a basis-dependent axis and changes under rephasing of Kramers pairs. However, the claimed commutation with the Dirac-Coulomb Hamiltonian is shown to be unfounded, invalidating the proposed quantum number.
AI.conclusion: The proposed quantum number -k^2 does not represent a genuine conserved quantity for the many-electron Dirac-Coulomb Hamiltonian. While the algebraic structure behind the reported spectrum is now understood, the physical claim of conservation fails, and the quantity should not be relied upon as a rigorous diagnostic.

title: Programmable Cavity Squeezing for Distributed Sensing in a Tweezer Array
summary: Field sensing with state-of-the-art atom interferometers is restricted to the use of uncorrelated devices op- erating in parallel. We can overcome this limitation by using distributed sensing protocols where quantum correlations among spatially-separated devices are engineered in the spatial mode carrying the signal. We show that a tweezer array in a cavity offers an ideal testbed to engineer quantum states for distributed sensing, with the possibility to generate entanglement both within and between the clouds. The competition between local and intercloud cavity-mediated exchange allows the sign and spatial pattern of the intercloud couplings to select the squeezed mode. For two ensembles, positive coupling produces uniform collective squeezing, whereas negative coupling generates strong staggered, nonlocal squeezing. A semiclassical analysis reveals a counter-twisting- like phase-space flow, qualitatively distinct from standard one-axis twisting. The analysis and results can be further generalized to a larger number of ensembles. We apply the scheme to differential Ramsey interferometry with common phase noise spanning the full 2 πrange, the resulting staggered states reduce the phase uncertainty below the standard quantum limit, with an ellipse estimator approaching the Cramèr-Rao bound. These results establish programmable cavity interactions as a scalable route to entanglement tailored to distributed signals.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using a tweezer array in a cavity to engineer distributed quantum sensing protocols, where cavity-mediated exchange couplings generate entanglement both within and between atomic ensembles. For two ensembles, positive coupling yields uniform collective squeezing while negative coupling produces strong staggered nonlocal squeezing. These states outperform the standard quantum limit in differential Ramsey interferometry, with phase uncertainties approaching the Cramèr-Rao bound.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art atom interferometers for field sensing are limited to uncorrelated devices operating in parallel, which restricts their sensitivity. The authors seek to overcome this by engineering quantum correlations among spatially separated devices in the spatial mode carrying the signal, enabling distributed sensing protocols.
AI.method: The authors use a tweezer array embedded in a cavity as a testbed for quantum state engineering. They analyze the competition between local and intercloud cavity-mediated exchange to control the sign and spatial pattern of couplings, thereby selecting the squeezed mode. A semiclassical analysis reveals a counter-twisting-like phase-space flow distinct from standard one-axis twisting, and the scheme is generalized to multiple ensembles.
AI.result: For two ensembles, positive intercloud coupling produces uniform collective squeezing, while negative coupling generates strong staggered nonlocal squeezing. Applied to differential Ramsey interferometry with common phase noise covering the full 2π range, the staggered states reduce phase uncertainty below the standard quantum limit, with an ellipse estimator approaching the Cramèr-Rao bound.
AI.conclusion: Programmable cavity interactions provide a scalable route to generating entanglement tailored to distributed signals, establishing a robust framework for distributed quantum sensing beyond the limitations of uncorrelated parallel devices.

title: Optimal Gaussian networks for private distributed quantum sensing
summary: Private distributed quantum sensing aims to estimate an authorized collective parameter while preventing independent estimation of individual local parameters. Here, we analytically characterize Gaussian quantum networks satisfying this perfect local privacy condition. Using a graph representation of the Gaussian pairing matrix, we show that two-mode squeezed vacuum states constitute the essential building blocks of privacy-preserving Gaussian states. We then analytically derive the optimal sensitivity under perfect local privacy and determine a Gaussian probe that achieves Heisenberg scaling with respect to both the photon number and the number of sensing modes. Using local homodyne measurements and maximum-likelihood estimation, we numerically verify quantum-enhanced sensitivity beyond the shot-noise limit while preserving perfect local privacy. We further show that the local-privacy condition is preserved under arbitrary phase-independent quantum channels, including optical loss. Our results provide a general framework for constructing and optimizing privacy-preserving continuous-variable quantum sensing networks.

AI.tldr: This paper analytically characterizes Gaussian quantum networks that achieve perfect local privacy in distributed quantum sensing, showing that two-mode squeezed vacuum states are the essential building blocks. The authors derive optimal sensitivity under perfect local privacy, achieving Heisenberg scaling in both photon number and number of sensing modes, and verify quantum-enhanced sensitivity numerically using homodyne measurements and maximum-likelihood estimation. The local-privacy condition is shown to be preserved under phase-independent quantum channels including optical loss.
AI.motivation: The goal is to enable private distributed quantum sensing where an authorized collective parameter can be estimated while preventing unauthorized estimation of individual local parameters, and to provide a general framework for constructing privacy-preserving continuous-variable quantum sensing networks.
AI.method: The authors use a graph representation of the Gaussian pairing matrix to characterize Gaussian quantum states satisfying perfect local privacy. They identify two-mode squeezed vacuum states as fundamental building blocks, analytically derive optimal sensitivity bounds under privacy constraints, and propose a Gaussian probe achieving Heisenberg scaling. Numerical verification is performed using local homodyne measurements with maximum-likelihood estimation.
AI.result: The optimal sensitivity under perfect local privacy is analytically derived, and a Gaussian probe achieving Heisenberg scaling with respect to both photon number and number of sensing modes is identified. Numerical results confirm quantum-enhanced sensitivity beyond the shot-noise limit while preserving perfect local privacy. The privacy condition is shown to persist under arbitrary phase-independent quantum channels, including optical loss.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a general framework for designing and optimizing privacy-preserving continuous-variable quantum sensing networks, with two-mode squeezed vacuum states as the core building blocks and robustness to realistic noise channels such as optical loss.

title: Dynamics and spectra of open quantum systems coupled to anharmonic environments
summary: In open quantum systems, the environment is typically modelled as a collection of harmonic oscillators, whereas realistic environments often exhibit unique non-Markovian effects due to the anharmonicity of the environment. Here we present a framework for modelling anharmonic environments in open quantum systems numerically exactly, in which, via a matching criterion, we map the anharmonic environment onto an effective harmonic one. This results in an effective spectral density that is a collection of shifted bare spectra arising from the non-equidistant energy gaps of the anharmonic environment, along with a unique zero-frequency term that effectively acts as static disorder on the system. This is due to the non-zero variance of the diagonal of the bath coupling operator. In tandem, we develop a framework for investigating the effects of environments comprising a few damped anharmonic modes where the matching criterion fails to work due to the non-Gaussianity of the environment. For both continuous and discrete damped anharmonic environments, this work investigates their unique influence on the system's dynamics, including enhanced non-Markovianity compared to a harmonic approximation, novel effects in the absorption spectrum, and the potential for anharmonic environments to enhance energy transport.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a numerically exact framework for modeling anharmonic environments in open quantum systems by mapping them onto effective harmonic ones via a matching criterion, yielding an effective spectral density of shifted bare spectra plus a static-disorder-like zero-frequency term. It also develops a framework for discrete damped anharmonic modes where the matching criterion fails due to non-Gaussianity, demonstrating enhanced non-Markovianity, novel absorption spectrum effects, and improved energy transport.
AI.motivation: Realistic environments in open quantum systems are often anharmonic, yet standard models assume collections of harmonic oscillators. This mismatch can miss unique non-Markovian effects arising from anharmonicity, motivating a numerically exact framework to capture these effects.
AI.method: The authors map an anharmonic environment onto an effective harmonic one using a matching criterion. This yields an effective spectral density composed of shifted bare spectra (from non-equidistant energy gaps) plus a zero-frequency term acting as static disorder due to the non-zero variance of the diagonal of the bath coupling operator. For discrete environments of few damped anharmonic modes where the matching criterion fails (due to non-Gaussianity), a separate framework is developed.
AI.result: For both continuous and discrete damped anharmonic environments, the work demonstrates unique influences on system dynamics: enhanced non-Markovianity relative to harmonic approximations, novel features in the absorption spectrum, and the potential for anharmonic environments to enhance energy transport.
AI.conclusion: Anharmonic environments can be treated numerically exactly via an effective harmonic mapping when the matching criterion holds, with a static-disorder contribution and shifted spectra. Where it fails, a tailored framework for few damped anharmonic modes is provided, revealing that anharmonicity can significantly alter quantum dynamics, including stronger non-Markovian behavior and improved energy transport.

title: Conditional contraction coefficients and their applications to quantum networks
summary: Contraction coefficients quantify the loss of distinguishability induced by a channel and provide a strong form of the data-processing inequality. While standard contraction coefficients ignore auxiliary quantum systems, existing extensions based on complete contraction coefficients require the compared states to have identical reference marginals. In this work, we introduce conditional contraction coefficients, a novel family that incorporates arbitrary quantum reference systems by subtracting the distinguishability already present in the reference system. We develop a general framework for contraction coefficients with such quantum side information, including the corresponding strong-data-processing-inequality (SDPI) constants, expansion coefficients, and relative contraction coefficients. For the trace distance, we show that the optimization can be restricted to orthogonal input states. For the quantum relative entropy, we prove that its conditional contraction coefficient is exactly equal to the contraction coefficient of the conditional mutual information, extending the classical correspondence between relative-entropy contraction and mutual-information contraction to the setting with quantum side information. More generally, we identify structural properties of divergences required for these results and discuss extensions beyond the relative entropy. These results establish a unified framework for analyzing information contraction in quantum network settings, where quantum side information and distributed correlations are intrinsic features of the information-processing task. Applications include an extension of the Polyanskiy-Wu bounds on mutual information contraction, new perspectives on mixing times, and fundamental limits on quantum memories.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces conditional contraction coefficients, a new family of contraction coefficients that accounts for arbitrary quantum reference systems by subtracting pre-existing distinguishability. It establishes a unified framework for strong data-processing inequalities with quantum side information, proves key structural results (orthogonal state optimization for trace distance, exact equivalence between relative-entropy and conditional-mutual-information contraction), and applies the framework to quantum network settings, mixing times, and quantum memory limits.
AI.motivation: Standard contraction coefficients measure information loss through channels but either ignore auxiliary quantum systems or require identical reference marginals in existing extensions. A framework is needed to handle arbitrary quantum side information, which is intrinsic to quantum network settings where distributed correlations are unavoidable.
AI.method: The authors define conditional contraction coefficients that subtract the distinguishability already present in the quantum reference system, and build a general framework including SDPI constants, expansion coefficients, and relative contraction coefficients. They prove structural theorems: for trace distance the optimization reduces to orthogonal input states; for quantum relative entropy, the conditional contraction coefficient exactly equals the contraction coefficient of conditional mutual information, extending classical correspondence results to quantum side information. They also identify the general structural properties of divergences needed for these results.
AI.result: Key results include: (1) reduction of trace-distance conditional contraction optimization to orthogonal inputs, (2) exact equality between the conditional contraction coefficient of quantum relative entropy and the contraction coefficient of conditional mutual information, (3) identification of general divergence structural properties enabling these results, and (4) applications extending Polyanskiy-Wu bounds to conditional mutual information contraction, providing new insights on mixing times and fundamental limits for quantum memories.
AI.conclusion: The framework unifies contraction analysis in quantum network settings with quantum side information, offering a principled tool for studying information-theoretic limits across quantum communication, memory, and mixing dynamics.

title: Strong Converse Exponent of Quantum State Merging
summary: We determine the strong converse exponent for the entanglement cost of quantum state merging, showing that it is characterized by the optimized $α$-$z$ conditional Rényi entropies with $z=α/2\in[1/2,1]$. This contrasts with the sandwiched conditional Rényi entropies that typically govern strong converse exponents in quantum information theory. As a consequence, we derive the strong converse exponent of the partially smoothed conditional min-entropy in purified distance. This exponent is governed by club-sandwiched conditional entropies, whereas global smoothing leads to a sandwiched expression.

AI.tldr: The paper determines the strong converse exponent for entanglement cost in quantum state merging, characterized by optimized α-z conditional Rényi entropies with z=α/2∈[1/2,1], and derives the strong converse exponent of partially smoothed conditional min-entropy in purified distance, governed by club-sandwiched conditional entropies.
AI.motivation: To characterize the strong converse exponents for quantum state merging, which is a fundamental primitive in quantum information theory, and to understand how different smoothing approaches (partial vs. global) affect the resulting exponents.
AI.method: The authors establish that the strong converse exponent for entanglement cost in state merging is governed by optimized α-z conditional Rényi entropies with the specific relation z=α/2, in contrast to the sandwiched conditional Rényi entropies typically used. They then leverage this result to derive the strong converse exponent of the partially smoothed conditional min-entropy in purified distance, revealing that partial smoothing leads to club-sandwiched conditional entropies while global smoothing yields a sandwiched expression.
AI.result: The main results are: (1) the strong converse exponent for entanglement cost in quantum state merging is characterized by optimized α-z conditional Rényi entropies with z=α/2∈[1/2,1]; (2) the strong converse exponent of the partially smoothed conditional min-entropy in purified distance is governed by club-sandwiched conditional entropies; (3) a contrast is shown between partial smoothing (yielding club-sandwiched entropies) and global smoothing (yielding sandwiched entropies).
AI.conclusion: The paper reveals an unexpected family of Rényi entropies governing strong converse exponents for state merging, demonstrating that the choice of smoothing (partial vs. global) qualitatively changes the mathematical structure of the resulting exponents.

title: The Find Rows and Columns and Decode algorithm for quantum expander codes
summary: A new adaptation of the Find Erasures and Decode algorithm from classical to quantum expander codes is presented. It runs in linear time and is parallelizable to logarithmic depth. Compared to Small Set Flip and Small Set Find, the new algorithm avoids the overhead of considering the subsets of stabilizer generators, requires less expansion and corrects more errors.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a new quantum expander code decoder adapted from the classical Find Erasures and Decode algorithm, running in linear time with logarithmic-depth parallelism, outperforming Small Set Flip and Small Set Find by avoiding subset overhead, requiring less expansion, and correcting more errors.
AI.motivation: To develop a more efficient and effective decoding algorithm for quantum expander codes that improves upon existing approaches like Small Set Flip and Small Set Find.
AI.method: Adapts the classical Find Erasures and Decode algorithm to the quantum expander code setting, designed to run in linear time and be parallelizable to logarithmic depth while avoiding the need to consider subsets of stabilizer generators.
AI.result: The new algorithm requires less expansion than Small Set Flip and Small Set Find, and corrects more errors, while maintaining linear time complexity and logarithmic-depth parallelizability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed quantum adaptation of Find Erasures and Decode offers a superior decoding approach for quantum expander codes with better error correction capability, reduced expansion requirements, and improved efficiency compared to prior methods.

title: Tight Bounds for Purity and Product Testing from Partial Transposition
summary: Coherent measurements across multiple copies of an unknown quantum state can substantially reduce the number of samples required to learn its properties, but remain experimentally challenging. Current experiments typically prepare and measure one copy at a time, potentially adapting later measurements to earlier outcomes. A central challenge is adaptivity, which makes the space of possible measurement strategies difficult to characterize. The positive-partial-transpose (PPT) relaxation bypasses this complexity by considering a larger, mathematically tractable class of measurements, at the risk of weakening the resulting bounds. Here we show, surprisingly, that the relaxation loses nothing at the level of asymptotic sample complexity for two fundamental tasks: purity testing and product testing. In both cases, lower bounds against the full class of PPT measurements are matched by nonadaptive single-copy protocols. Moreover, our proof requires only basic symmetric subspace identities, providing a simple route to sharp lower bounds for adaptive single-copy measurements.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the PPT relaxation, a mathematically tractable class of measurements that includes adaptive strategies, provides asymptotically tight sample complexity bounds for purity testing and product testing. In both tasks, lower bounds against all PPT measurements are matched by nonadaptive single-copy protocols, and the proof requires only basic symmetric subspace identities.
AI.motivation: Adaptivity in quantum measurement strategies makes the space of possible protocols difficult to characterize, yet this is a core challenge for learning properties of unknown quantum states. The PPT relaxation offers a tractable alternative but risks weakening bounds. The authors aim to determine whether this relaxation remains meaningful for fundamental learning tasks.
AI.method: The authors analyze the asymptotic sample complexity of purity testing and product testing using the PPT relaxation framework. They prove that lower bounds derived against the full class of PPT measurements are matched by explicit nonadaptive single-copy protocols, and derive these results using basic symmetric subspace identities.
AI.result: The PPT relaxation loses nothing at the level of asymptotic sample complexity for both purity testing and product testing. The relaxation-based lower bounds are tight and achieved by simple nonadaptive single-copy strategies, giving sharp lower bounds for adaptive single-copy measurements.
AI.conclusion: The PPT relaxation is asymptotically optimal for purity testing and product testing, and the proofs are surprisingly simple, requiring only elementary symmetric subspace identities. This provides a clean route to establishing sharp lower bounds for adaptive single-copy quantum measurements in these tasks.

title: Efficient formation and identification of single emitters in 4H-SiC following maskless heavy ion implantation
summary: Single photon emitters in silicon carbide (SiC) are a leading platform for scalable quantum technologies. Recent interest has focused on oxygen-vacancy-related emitters, which show exceptionally high optical brightness and strong spin readout contrast. One barrier to scalable quantum devices based on these emitters is the challenge of maskless formation and rapid identification. Here, we demonstrate the formation of isolated bright single emitters in 4H-SiC, using low-energy maskless implantation of heavy ions bismuth and tin. Following annealing, up to 18% of implanted sites host a single emitter, with optimal yields achieved at annealing temperatures of 900-1000 degrees C. Occupancy statistics are modelled to estimate the implantation dose that maximises single-emitter yield. We introduce a tiered characterisation scheme, where a simple intensity threshold isolates single-emitter candidates, confirmed through photon correlation measurements, after which correlations between polarisation, saturation count rate and magnetic resonance frequency assign emitter type. It is shown that time-consuming low-temperature spectroscopy is not necessary to distinguish emitter types. Together, maskless heavy-ion implantation and selective screening offer an efficient route to forming and rapidly identifying near-surface single emitters for room-temperature quantum technologies such as quantum sensing.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates the maskless formation of isolated bright single emitters in 4H-SiC using low-energy heavy-ion (bismuth and tin) implantation, achieving up to 18% single-emitter yields after annealing at 900-1000°C. The authors introduce a tiered characterization scheme using intensity thresholds, photon correlation, and correlations between polarization, saturation count rate, and magnetic resonance frequency to rapidly identify emitter types without time-consuming low-temperature spectroscopy.
AI.motivation: Oxygen-vacancy-related single photon emitters in SiC show exceptional optical brightness and spin readout contrast, making them promising for scalable quantum technologies. However, maskless formation and rapid identification of these emitters remain a barrier to scalable quantum devices.
AI.method: Low-energy maskless implantation of heavy ions (bismuth and tin) into 4H-SiC, followed by annealing at 900-1000°C. Occupancy statistics were modeled to estimate optimal implantation dose. A tiered characterization scheme was introduced: (1) intensity threshold filtering to isolate single-emitter candidates, (2) photon correlation measurements for confirmation, and (3) correlations between polarization, saturation count rate, and magnetic resonance frequency to assign emitter type.
AI.result: Up to 18% of implanted sites hosted a single emitter, with optimal yields at annealing temperatures of 900-1000°C. The tiered characterization scheme successfully distinguished emitter types without requiring low-temperature spectroscopy.
AI.conclusion: Combining maskless heavy-ion implantation with selective screening provides an efficient route to forming and rapidly identifying near-surface single emitters suitable for room-temperature quantum technologies such as quantum sensing.

title: Optimal cloning of mixed states
summary:
We consider the problem of approximate cloning of quantum states: given $n$ copies of an unknown state $ρ\in \mathbb{C}^{d \times d}$, prepare an $(n+k)$-copy state with high fidelity to $ρ^{\otimes (n+k)}$. Werner's pure state cloner is the optimal channel for the pure state case, and shows that $n = Θ(kd/\varepsilon)$ copies are necessary and sufficient to clone $k$ additional copies of an unknown pure state to fidelity $1-\varepsilon$. The random purification channel gives a straightforward extension of Werner's cloner to mixed state inputs: given $n$ copies of a mixed state, randomly purify your input, apply Werner's channel in the larger Hilbert space, and then trace out the auxiliary registers. This gives a mixed state cloner using $n = O(krd/\varepsilon)$ copies to clone rank-$r$ states. Can one do any better? We show that the answer is no: one must use $n = Ω(krd/\varepsilon)$ copies. We prove our lower bound by studying the special case of projector cloning, in which the input state $ρ$ is promised to be of the form $P/r$, where $P$ is a rank-$r$ orthogonal projector.
  As a further application of our techniques, we consider the closely related problem of approximate transposition of quantum states, where one seeks to convert $ρ^{\otimes n}$ to a $k$-copy state with high fidelity to $(ρ^T)^{\otimes k}$. Here, we again show $n = Θ(krd/\varepsilon)$ copies are necessary and sufficient for this task.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes tight bounds for approximate quantum state cloning and transposition of mixed states. For cloning rank-r density matrices (dimension d) to fidelity 1-ε, n = Θ(krd/ε) copies are necessary and sufficient, matching the performance of the random purification channel. The same tight bound holds for approximate transposition.
AI.motivation: While Werner's pure state cloner and its extension to mixed states via the random purification channel give an upper bound of n = O(krd/ε) copies for mixed state cloning, it was unknown whether this could be improved. The paper aims to resolve this question by establishing a matching lower bound.
AI.method: The authors prove the lower bound by analyzing the special case of projector cloning, where the input is promised to be P/r for a rank-r orthogonal projector P. The same techniques are then applied to the closely related problem of approximate transposition of quantum states.
AI.result: The paper shows that n = Ω(krd/ε) copies are necessary for mixed state cloning, matching the O(krd/ε) upper bound from the random purification channel, thus establishing the optimal complexity as Θ(krd/ε). For approximate transposition, the same tight bound n = Θ(krd/ε) is shown.
AI.conclusion: The random purification channel achieves the optimal sample complexity for mixed state cloning, and no better strategy exists. The techniques developed for proving this lower bound also yield tight bounds for approximate quantum transposition, resolving both problems.

title: The Geometry of Dissipative Complexity: A Levi-Type Decomposition Theorem for Markovian Quantum Dynamics via Lie Wedges and Invariant Cones
summary:
Lie algebras describe how control Hamiltonians combine in closed quantum systems. In open Markovian systems, however, dissipation introduces irreversible directions that the Lie algebra alone does not retain. A dynamical Lie wedge preserves this information as a convex cone of locally admissible generators. The classical Levi decomposition separates a finite-dimensional Lie algebra into semisimple and solvable parts. In this work, we prove a corresponding decomposition and reconstruction theorem for dynamical Lie wedges.
  The theorem decomposes the wedge into semisimple and solvable data, records how these components are coupled, and provides a converse reconstruction of the wedge.
