The framework yields four structural types of the generated algebra. We further prove that the total dissipation strength of every admissible generator depends only on its coordinate in the solvable radical. In particular, if the generated Lie algebra is semisimple, every admissible generator is Hamiltonian. Together, these results extend Lie-algebraic structural methods to irreversible Markovian control and clarify how dissipation is encoded in the generator geometry.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a Levi-type decomposition and reconstruction theorem for dynamical Lie wedges in open Markovian quantum systems, decomposing the wedge into semisimple and solvable components and showing that dissipation strength depends only on the solvable radical coordinates.
AI.motivation: Lie algebras capture how control Hamiltonians combine in closed quantum systems but fail to describe irreversible directions introduced by dissipation in open Markovian systems. A dynamical Lie wedge preserves this information as a convex cone of locally admissible generators, yet no structural decomposition theorem analogous to Levi decomposition existed for such wedges.
AI.method: The authors prove a decomposition and reconstruction theorem for dynamical Lie wedges that separates the wedge into semisimple and solvable data, records how these components couple, and provides a converse reconstruction procedure. The framework classifies generated algebras into four structural types.
AI.result: The theorem yields four structural types of the generated algebra. The paper proves that total dissipation strength of every admissible generator depends only on its coordinates in the solvable radical. If the generated Lie algebra is semisimple, every admissible generator is Hamiltonian.
AI.conclusion: These results extend Lie-algebraic structural methods to irreversible Markovian control, clarifying how dissipation is encoded in generator geometry and enabling structural analysis of open quantum control systems.

title: Evaluating Quantum Kernel Methods for Track-Based Classification in High-Energy Physics
summary:
We present a systematic design for large-scale quantum kernel classification, demonstrated through a quantum support vector classifier (QSVC) for particle-track classification using centroid-based CLAS12 drift-chamber features. Each event is encoded into a six-qubit state via a fully entangled ZZFeatureMap, whose fidelities define a quantum kernel within a standard SVM framework. By decoupling state preparation from kernel construction and distributing evaluation across a multi-node MPI-based HPC allocation, the approach scales to 1.0x10^5 training and 4.0x10^5 test events with an exactly constructed kernel matrix, to our knowledge more than an order of magnitude larger than prior high-energy-physics quantum-kernel studies.
  Benchmarked against linear, polynomial, RBF, and sigmoid SVM kernels and extremely randomized trees (ERT), the ideal QSVC achieves the highest recall (99.99%) among all models. Under a calibrated hardware noise model (FakeMumbaiV2, 500 training / 2,000 test events), AUC falls from 0.9985 to 0.9671 and peak significance improvement falls from 17.5 to ~3.5, yet recall remains at 99.51% -- indicating this signal-retention advantage is attenuated but not eliminated by circuit-level decoherence.
  Geometric analysis of the quantum embedding shows near-orthogonal inter-class states with coherent intra-class neighborhoods under ideal simulation; under noise this structure compresses toward the maximally mixed state while preserving its relative ordering.
  These results demonstrate a scalable, reproducible workflow for quantum kernel experimentation at HEP-relevant scale, quantifying the practical cost of realistic hardware noise on quantum-enhanced classification.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a systematic, scalable design for quantum kernel classification applied to particle-track classification in high-energy physics, using a six-qubit ZZFeatureMap embedded in a quantum support vector classifier (QSVC). The approach scales to 1.0×10^5 training and 4.0×10^5 test events with an exactly constructed kernel matrix—over an order of magnitude larger than prior HEP quantum-kernel studies. Under ideal simulation, QSVC achieves 99.99% recall, outperforming classical baselines; under realistic hardware noise, AUC degrades from 0.9985 to 0.9671 but recall remains at 99.51%, showing noise attenuates but does not eliminate the quantum advantage. Geometric analysis reveals the coherent structure of the quantum embedding compresses toward the maximally mixed state under noise while preserving relative inter-class ordering.
AI.motivation: Quantum kernel methods hold promise for enhancing classification tasks in high-energy physics (HEP), but prior studies have been limited to small dataset scales and have not systematically quantified the impact of real hardware noise. The authors aim to demonstrate a scalable and reproducible workflow for quantum kernel experimentation at HEP-relevant scale, while quantifying the practical cost of realistic hardware decoherence on quantum-enhanced classification.
AI.method: Each event is encoded into a six-qubit state via a fully entangled ZZFeatureMap, whose fidelities form a quantum kernel used within a standard SVM framework. State preparation is decoupled from kernel construction, and evaluation is distributed across a multi-node MPI-based HPC allocation, enabling an exactly constructed kernel matrix at scale (1.0×10^5 training / 4.0×10^5 test events). Benchmarks compare against classical SVM kernels (linear, polynomial, RBF, sigmoid) and extremely randomized trees. Robustness is assessed under a calibrated hardware noise model (FakeMumbaiV2) at reduced scale, with geometric analysis of the quantum embedding under ideal and noisy conditions.
AI.result: The ideal QSVC achieves the highest recall (99.99%) among all models tested. Under FakeMumbaiV2 noise (500 training / 2,000 test events), AUC drops from 0.9985 to 0.9671 and peak significance improvement falls from 17.5 to ~3.5, yet recall remains at 99.51%. Geometric analysis shows near-orthogonal inter-class states with coherent intra-class neighborhoods under ideal simulation; under noise, this structure compresses toward the maximally mixed state while preserving relative ordering.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates a scalable and reproducible workflow for quantum kernel classification at HEP-relevant scale. While realistic hardware noise significantly degrades performance metrics (AUC and significance), the signal-retention advantage (high recall) persists, suggesting that quantum-enhanced classification remains viable but requires noise mitigation for practical deployment.

title: Dynamics-based nonclassicality witness under dissipative dynamics
summary: A dynamics-based test, originally proposed by Tsirelson for the harmonic oscillator, provides a method for certifying quantumness under the assumption of a known Hamiltonian. These tests, however, are typically proposed for isolated systems, an assumption that breaks down in experimental implementation. In this paper, we extend the protocol to the harmonic oscillator coupled to standard models of dissipation: thermal relaxation, pure dephasing, and the Caldeira--Leggett model. Using the Moyal-Wigner formalism of quantum mechanics in phase space, we show that the introduction of dissipation requires a dissipation-dependent shift of the classical bound, and provide the threshold under which the nonclassicality witness retains its validity.

AI.tldr: This paper extends Tsirelson's dynamics-based quantumness test to driven harmonic oscillators coupled to dissipative environments (thermal relaxation, pure dephasing, and the Caldeira-Leggett model), showing that dissipation introduces a shift in the classical bound and providing the threshold where the nonclassicality witness remains valid.
AI.motivation: Original quantumness certification tests are designed for isolated systems, which breaks down in real experimental settings where dissipation is unavoidable. The authors aim to make dynamics-based nonclassicality tests robust to realistic environmental effects.
AI.method: The authors use the Moyal-Wigner phase-space formalism of quantum mechanics to analyze the dynamics-based test when the harmonic oscillator is coupled to standard dissipation models, deriving a dissipation-dependent correction to the classical bound.
AI.result: The introduction of dissipation requires a dissipation-dependent shift of the classical bound for the quantumness test, and explicit thresholds are provided below which the nonclassicality witness remains valid.
AI.conclusion: The dynamics-based quantumness certification protocol can be adapted to open quantum systems by accounting for dissipation-induced shifts in the classical bound, extending the test's applicability to realistic experimental conditions.

title: Quantum Chaos and Quantum Optimal Transport
summary: Chaos in classical systems can be characterized by Lyapunov exponents that measure the exponential divergence of nearby trajectories, but directly extending this framework to quantum mechanics has been a persistent challenge. The wavelike nature of quantum states and the non-commutative geometry of quantum phase space obstruct a straightforward generalization of classical chaos theory. Here we develop a rigorous approach to quantum chaos by leveraging quantum optimal transport theory, which provides the missing geometric foundation for measuring distances between extended quantum distributions. We define quantum Lyapunov exponents that naturally avoid divergences encountered when naïvely generalizing classical exponents, and show that in the semiclassical limit they recover the classical global expansion rate, and hence the usual maximal Lyapunov exponent when they coincide. Our framework provides a tight connection between the divergence of classical trajectories and semiclassical phase space evolution, and additionally clarifies the role of out-of-time-order correlators as diagnostics of quantum chaos. These results establish quantum optimal transport as a unifying mathematical foundation for quantum chaos theory, providing new tools to characterize dynamical behavior across the full range of quantum dynamics from simple few-body models to complex many-body systems.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a rigorous framework for quantum chaos by using quantum optimal transport theory to define quantum Lyapunov exponents that avoid divergences in naive generalizations, recover classical expansion rates in the semiclassical limit, and connect classical trajectory divergence with semiclassical phase space evolution while clarifying the role of out-of-time-order correlators.
AI.motivation: Directly extending classical chaos theory based on Lyapunov exponents to quantum mechanics has been a persistent challenge due to the wavelike nature of quantum states and the non-commutative geometry of quantum phase space, obstructing a straightforward generalization.
AI.method: The authors leverage quantum optimal transport theory to provide a geometric foundation for measuring distances between extended quantum distributions, and use it to define quantum Lyapunov exponents that rigorously capture chaotic behavior in quantum systems.
AI.result: The quantum Lyapunov exponents avoid divergences encountered in naive generalizations, recover the classical global expansion rate and maximal Lyapunov exponent in the semiclassical limit, and provide a tight connection between classical trajectory divergence and semiclassical phase space evolution while clarifying the role of out-of-time-order correlators.
AI.conclusion: Quantum optimal transport serves as a unifying mathematical foundation for quantum chaos theory, providing new tools to characterize dynamical behavior across the full range of quantum dynamics from few-body to many-body systems.

title: Randomness can be certified in energy-constrained semi-device-independent scenarios
summary:
The prepare-and-measure framework based on energy constraints offers a practical middle ground between fully device-dependent and device-independent quantum cryptography. The only assumption on an otherwise uncharacterized prepare-and-measure device is that the energy of the prepared states is bounded. Existing security analyses of this framework assume that the preparation and measurement devices share at most classical correlations, and under this assumption certified lower bounds on the extractable randomness have been established. Recent work has shown that an adversary who pre-distributes entanglement between the devices can mount attacks that are strictly more powerful than those available when the devices share only classical correlations, reducing the extractable randomness below the previously certified rates. This leaves open the fundamental question of whether randomness can be certified at all in this scenario.
  We address this open question by constructing semidefinite programming relaxations of the guessing probability by adapting the Navascués-Pironio-Acín hierarchy to the energy-constrained setting where shared entanglement between the devices is permitted. Our relaxations yield certified lower bounds on the extractable randomness without enforcing any restrictions on the dimensions of the quantum state shared between the preparation and measurement devices. We show that these certified lower bounds are strictly positive for a range of energy values, thereby answering the open question affirmatively: certified randomness generation is theoretically possible in the energy-constrained SDI framework even in the presence of a fully quantum adversary.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that certified randomness generation is possible in the energy-constrained semi-device-independent (SDI) prepare-and-measure framework even when the preparation and measurement devices share entanglement with a fully quantum adversary, by constructing semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations based on a Navascués-Pironio-Acín (NPA) hierarchy adapted to energy constraints.
AI.motivation: The energy-constrained prepare-and-measure framework is a practical middle ground between fully device-dependent and device-independent quantum cryptography. Previous security analyses only assumed classical correlations between devices, but recent work showed that an adversary pre-distributing entanglement between devices can mount strictly more powerful attacks, reducing extractable randomness below previously certified rates. This left open whether randomness can be certified at all in this scenario—a fundamental question this paper addresses.
AI.method: The authors construct semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations of the guessing probability by adapting the Navascués-Pironio-Acín (NPA) hierarchy to the energy-constrained setting where shared entanglement between the preparation and measurement devices is permitted. The relaxations avoid enforcing any restrictions on the dimensions of the quantum state shared between the devices.
AI.result: The SDP relaxations yield certified lower bounds on extractable randomness that are shown to be strictly positive for a range of energy values, thereby providing affirmative evidence that certified randomness generation is theoretically possible in the energy-constrained SDI framework under a fully quantum (entanglement-sharing) adversary.
AI.conclusion: Certified randomness generation is theoretically possible in the energy-constrained semi-device-independent framework even in the presence of a fully quantum adversary who shares entanglement between the preparation and measurement devices—answering the open question affirmatively.

title: On supporting affine functionals for Entanglement of Formation
comment: 14 pages, preliminary version, any comments are welcome
summary:
In several articles, the authors assume that the convex roof structure of the EoF and finite-dimensionality of subsystems $A$ and $B$ guarantee the existence of the (global) supporting affine functional for the EoF at any state of the system $AB$. This means that for any state $ρ$ of $AB$ there is a Hermitian operator $Λ_ρ$ on $\mathcal{H}_{AB}=\mathcal{H}_A\otimes\mathcal{H}_B$ such that $E_F(ρ)=\mathrm{Tr}Λ_ρρ$ and $E_F(σ)\geq\mathrm{Tr}Λ_ρσ$ for any state $σ$ of $AB$. We present an explicit example showing that, when $ρ$ is degenerate, this is not true even in the simplest case when $A$ and $B$ are qubit systems. The construction is based on the fact that the existence of a supporting affine functional for the EoF at a state $ρ$ is equivalent to the Lipschitz lower semicontinuity of the EoF at this state $ρ$. We use Wootters' formula and the help of Claude Fable 5 to find a state $ρ$ of the system $AB$ for which the latter property does not hold.
  We also describe conditions for the existence the local and global supporting affine functionals for the EoF at a given state of both finite and infinite-dimensional bipartite quantum systems. These conditions allow us to find Lipschitz lower semicontinuity bounds for the EoF at a given finite rank state $ρ$ (i.e. inequalities of the form $\,E_F(ρ)-E_F(σ)\leq C_ρ\|ρ-σ\|_1$) with and without restrictions on the support of the state $σ$.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges a widely used assumption that the convex roof structure and finite-dimensionality of subsystems guarantee the existence of a global supporting affine functional for the Entanglement of Formation (EoF) at any state. The authors provide a counterexample showing this fails for degenerate states even in the simplest qubit-qubit case, using the equivalence between supporting affine functionals and Lipschitz lower semicontinuity. They also establish general conditions for the existence of local and global supporting affine functionals for both finite and infinite-dimensional bipartite systems, yielding Lipschitz lower semicontinuity bounds for finite rank states.
AI.motivation: Several articles rely on the assumption that a global supporting affine functional for the EoF always exists at any state of a bipartite system with finite-dimensional subsystems. The authors aim to verify this assumption and demonstrate that it is false for degenerate states, even in the simplest qubit-qubit case.
AI.method: The authors exploit the equivalence between the existence of a supporting affine functional for the EoF at a state ρ and the Lipschitz lower semicontinuity of the EoF at ρ. They use Wootters' formula (for qubit systems) and computational assistance (Claude Fable 5) to construct a counterexample. They also derive general conditions for the existence of local and global supporting affine functionals applicable to both finite and infinite-dimensional bipartite systems.
AI.result: An explicit counterexample is constructed showing that the assumed existence of a global supporting affine functional fails for degenerate states even when both subsystems are qubits. The paper also provides conditions for existence of supporting affine functionals and derives Lipschitz lower semicontinuity bounds for the EoF at finite rank states, with and without support restrictions on the comparison state σ.
AI.conclusion: The commonly assumed existence of global supporting affine functionals for the EoF is not guaranteed for degenerate states, requiring more careful treatment in proofs that rely on this assumption. The new conditions and bounds provided fill this gap and apply to both finite and infinite-dimensional bipartite quantum systems.

title: Stochastic transport of a Goldstone mode in a self-organized atomic crystal
summary: Spontaneous breaking of a continuous symmetry produces a massless Goldstone mode that can evolve across a degenerate manifold at zero energy cost. Goldstone modes have been identified primarily through excitation spectra, mode softening or collective oscillations. However, their time-domain transport under intrinsic fluctuations and dissipation has remained largely unexplored. Here we directly track the stochastic transport of a Goldstone mode in a self-organized atomic crystal inside an optical ring cavity. The ring cavity maps the order-parameter phase onto the real-space position of the emergent crystal. Without any external perturbation, fundamental photon-scattering recoil drives the collective transport, while cavity dissipation generates friction. We monitor individual trajectories of the atoms and their self-generated optical lattice by measuring the cavity output phase. We find that the diffusion constant decreases as $1/N$, indicating that all atoms move collectively as a rigid object rather than independently. By tuning the Langevin driving force and cavity-mediated damping, we show that the normalized diffusion constant collapses onto a single universal curve. This work extends the study of continuous symmetry breaking from excitation-frequency measurements to real-time tracking of transport, and opens routes for studying non-equilibrium collective transport, phonon dynamics, and defect formation in driven-dissipative quantum matter.

AI.tldr: The paper directly tracks the stochastic, time-domain transport of a Goldstone mode in a self-organized atomic crystal inside an optical ring cavity, showing that all atoms move collectively as a rigid object (diffusion scales as 1/N) and that normalized diffusion collapses onto a universal curve as a function of Langevin driving and cavity-mediated damping.
AI.motivation: Goldstone modes have been identified primarily through excitation spectra, mode softening, or collective oscillations, but their time-domain transport under intrinsic fluctuations and dissipation has remained largely unexplored.
AI.method: A self-organized atomic crystal is created inside an optical ring cavity. The ring cavity maps the order-parameter phase onto the real-space position of the emergent crystal. Individual atom trajectories and the self-generated optical lattice are monitored by measuring the cavity output phase. Photon-scattering recoil drives collective transport, while cavity dissipation provides friction. The Langevin driving force and cavity-mediated damping are tuned to study the normalized diffusion constant.
AI.result: The diffusion constant decreases as 1/N, indicating all atoms move collectively as a rigid object rather than independently. The normalized diffusion constant collapses onto a single universal curve when the Langevin driving force and cavity-mediated damping are tuned.
AI.conclusion: This work extends the study of continuous symmetry breaking from excitation-frequency measurements to real-time tracking of transport, and opens routes for studying non-equilibrium collective transport, phonon dynamics, and defect formation in driven-dissipative quantum matter.

title: Detuning- and Stark-robust Rydberg gates
comment: E.B. and G.N contributed equally to this work
summary: Rydberg entangling gates driven by a two-photon transition in alkali atoms suffer from an adverse scaling of light-shift-induced errors. Robustness to such detuning errors is known to be impossible to achieve in the design of conventional Rydberg gate protocols, where only one of the qubit states is coupled to the Rydberg state. Here, we show that in a more general framework, in which both qubit states take part in the gate, full or partial robustness to these errors can be realized. We present two gate constructions, which either cancel the errors outright or convert them into single-qubit errors that can be corrected locally. We map the regimes -- in terms of light-shift strength, intensity inhomogeneity, and Rydberg decay rate -- in which these protocols outperform the widely used time-optimal Rydberg gate, and find that they already include the conditions of state-of-the-art experiments. Finally, we show the existence of a Rydberg `fly-by' entangling gate, an important primitive for an emerging class of neutral-atom quantum computing architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that Rydberg entangling gates can achieve full or partial robustness to light-shift-induced errors when both qubit states participate in the gate, unlike conventional protocols where only one qubit state couples to the Rydberg state. Two gate constructions are presented—one canceling errors outright and another converting them into locally correctable single-qubit errors—and the authors map the parameter regimes where these outperform time-optimal Rydberg gates, including conditions matching state-of-the-art experiments. A novel Rydberg 'fly-by' entangling gate for emerging neutral-atom quantum computing architectures is also introduced.
AI.motivation: Two-photon Rydberg entangling gates in alkali atoms suffer from adverse light-shift-induced detuning errors. Conventional Rydberg gate protocols, where only one qubit state is coupled to the Rydberg state, are known to be unable to achieve robustness to these errors, motivating a search for more general gate designs.
AI.method: The authors generalize the Rydberg gate framework to allow both qubit states to participate in the gate. They present two gate constructions: one that fully cancels light-shift errors and another that converts them into locally correctable single-qubit errors. They analyze the performance across parameter regimes (light-shift strength, intensity inhomogeneity, Rydberg decay rate) and introduce a Rydberg 'fly-by' gate for advancing neutral-atom architectures.
AI.result: The proposed protocols outperform the standard time-optimal Rydberg gate in regimes that already include conditions of state-of-the-art experiments. Both full cancellation and error conversion to correctable single-qubit errors are achieved, and the feasibility of a Rydberg 'fly-by' entangling gate is demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: By allowing both qubit states to participate in Rydberg gate dynamics, robustness to light-shift errors becomes achievable—something impossible with conventional single-state-coupled protocols. This opens new design avenues and supports emerging neutral-atom quantum computing architectures, including fly-by gates.

title: Factorized Boolean representations for efficient quantum synthesis
summary: Quantum algorithms promise advantages beyond classical reach, but running them on error-corrected hardware requires translating Boolean specifications into reversible circuits, and the resources that translation demands determine what is executable. Established methods minimize a Boolean expression and map it to a circuit, assuming the minimized form is best. Here we show that minimized expressions retain algebraic structure minimization cannot reach, arising from containment and complementary-polarity relationships among their terms, and that extracting it yields circuits cheaper to execute despite having more operations. The decisive quantity is not a circuit's operation count but the control count of its widest operation, a superlinear cost; extracting shared factors trades a few wide operations for many narrow ones and reduces qubit count. Across benchmarks and oracles from quantum search and factoring algorithms, at the representation level the transformation never increases either cost measure, a guarantee from its construction. Translation to an executable circuit returns part of that advantage, since auxiliary lines must be uncomputed, yet the factorized circuit still left a leading circuit-level optimizer reaching lower final counts, and faster, than unaided. The representation of a computation is therefore itself a resource, optimizable before compilation and distinct from both logic minimization and circuit-level optimization.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that minimized Boolean expressions retain exploitable algebraic structure—containment and complementary-polarity relationships among terms—that logic minimization cannot reach. Extracting these shared factors yields circuits with more operations but lower control counts on the widest operation (a superlinear cost), reducing qubit count. Across benchmarks and quantum oracles, the transformation never increases either cost measure at the representation level, and after translation to executable circuits, a leading circuit-level optimizer reaches lower final counts faster than unaided. The representation itself is thus a resource, optimizable before compilation and distinct from both logic minimization and circuit-level optimization.
AI.motivation: Established methods for compiling Boolean specifications into reversible quantum circuits assume that minimizing the Boolean expression is the best path. The authors hypothesize that minimized expressions still retain algebraic structure (containment and complementary-polarity relationships) that minimization cannot capture, and that exploiting this structure yields cheaper circuits despite having more operations.
AI.method: The authors identify and extract shared factors arising from containment and complementary-polarity relationships among terms in minimized Boolean expressions. The key optimization metric is not operation count but the control count of the widest operation (a superlinear cost). The transformation trades a few wide operations for many narrow ones, reducing qubit count. The method is validated on benchmarks and oracles from quantum search and factoring algorithms.
AI.result: At the representation level, the transformation never increases either cost measure, a guarantee from its construction. When translated to executable circuits (where auxiliary lines must be uncomputed), part of the advantage is returned, yet the factorized circuit still allowed a leading circuit-level optimizer to reach lower final counts, and faster, than when run unaided.
AI.conclusion: The representation of a computation is itself a resource that is optimizable before compilation, distinct from both logic minimization and circuit-level optimization. Extracting algebraic structure from minimized expressions yields circuits that are cheaper to execute despite having more operations.

title: Spectral Fingerprints of Gauge Theories on a Quantum Computer
summary: Maximally mixed state spectral sampling is an unbiased quantum algorithm that allows for extraction of a finite-resolution spectral distribution from a Hamiltonian over potentially the entire allowed range of energies. We show how it may be focused on any desired area of the spectrum in order to learn about the full \textit{fingerprint} of the model of interest: from its ground state phenomena such as quantum criticality, obtained from the lowest lying energies, to its thermalization behavior, obtained from the mid-spectrum. We demonstrate this technique specifically on a $(1+1)d$ non-Abelian $SO(3)$ gauge theory, providing a comprehensive analysis of the steps necessary for performing this algorithm, as well as what is possible in the near-term with superconducting quantum hardware, performing simulations with circuits that are $78$ two-qubit gates deep. We show how this algorithm is able to take advantage of emerging dynamical circuit capabilities in near-term hardware to roughly halve the number required qubits, as well as how quantum readout error mitigation is trivial for this method. Along the way, we propose a novel strategy for compiling the controlled-time evolutions needed for spectral sampling by means of Pauli-frame optimizations. We illustrate two physical applications of quantum spectral sampling -- disordered many-body transitions, and mid-spectrum densities of states -- and what postprocessing steps they require beyond the Fourier outputs of the algorithm.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a generalized approach to maximally mixed state spectral sampling, a quantum algorithm that extracts a finite-resolution energy spectrum, and demonstrates it on a (1+1)d non-Abelian SO(3) gauge theory using circuits 78 two-qubit gates deep, with techniques to halve qubit requirements via dynamical circuits and trivial readout error mitigation.
AI.motivation: Spectral sampling for energy distributions is typically limited to near-ground-state energies. The authors aim to extend this technique to focus on any desired spectral region—from ground-state physics like quantum criticality to thermalization behavior in the mid-spectrum—enabling a full spectral "fingerprint" of quantum models, particularly relevant for lattice gauge theories.
AI.method: The algorithm uses maximally mixed state spectral sampling, a resolution-limited unbiased quantum algorithm. The authors demonstrate it on a (1+1)d non-Abelian SO(3) gauge theory, exploiting dynamical circuit capabilities to halve qubit count, using a novel Pauli-frame optimization strategy for compiling controlled time evolutions, and leveraging trivial quantum readout error mitigation inherent to the method.
AI.result: Simulations were performed with circuits 78 two-qubit gates deep on superconducting quantum hardware. The algorithm successfully extracts spectral information across the full energy range and supports physical applications including disordered many-body transitions and mid-spectrum densities of states, with specific postprocessing requirements beyond Fourier outputs.
AI.conclusion: Maximally mixed state spectral sampling is a versatile near-term quantum algorithm capable of probing the full spectral fingerprint of quantum many-body systems, and is feasible on current superconducting hardware with practical resource reductions from dynamical circuits and error mitigation.
